data.title: Kinnevik Q3 2026 slides: NAV rises 1% as portfolio diverges
data.ai_summary: Kinnevik reported Q3 2026 results on October 15, with NAV rising 1% to SEK 29.8 billion despite portfolio divergence. Health and bio holdings gained, offset by software valuation pressure, while shares fell 6.01% in premarket trading. The company maintains SEK 7.4 billion in net cash and a 19% total shareholder return.
data.full_text:
Asia stocks tumble as South Korea’s KOSPI triggers circuit breaker in tech rout
Introduction & Market Context
Swedish investment company Kinnevik presented its third quarter 2026 results on October 15, reporting net asset value growth of 1% to SEK 29.8 billion despite divergent performance across its portfolio. The presentation revealed gains in health and bio holdings offset by valuation pressure in software companies, while the shares fell 6.01% to $65.63 in premarket trading as investors weighed multiple compression concerns against a strong balance sheet.
The company maintained net cash of SEK 7.4 billion and delivered a 19% total shareholder return during the quarter, significantly outpacing the OMXSGI index’s 2% return. However, the stock remains well below its 52-week high of $91.15, reflecting ongoing market scrutiny of private market valuations.
Quarterly Performance Highlights
As shown in the following summary of key financial metrics, Kinnevik deployed SEK 165 million in new investments while realizing SEK 183 million from divestments during the quarter.
The company’s net asset value progression from SEK 29.6 billion in Q2 to SEK 29.8 billion in Q3 was driven by several offsetting factors. The following waterfall chart illustrates how various drivers impacted NAV during the quarter.
The NAV development reflected a 3% increase from improved near-term outlook, driven by broad-based growth across portfolio companies and Cityblock’s strategic acquisition of Homeward Health. This was partially offset by a 2% decline from multiple compression, as updated forward growth expectations held multiples back relative to peers in certain subsectors. Currency movements contributed a positive 2% impact as the Swedish krona weakened against the dollar and euro, while cash flow and dilution effects created modest headwinds.
Three portfolio companies achieved significant milestones during the quarter, as illustrated in the following breakdown of key events.
Tandem Health raised USD 100 million in new funding and is now integrated with over 130 medical record systems across 14 European markets. Enveda secured USD 311 million while advancing three clinical programs in atopic dermatitis, metabolic health and inflammatory bowel disease. Cityblock raised USD 116 million and acquired Homeward, expanding to nearly 200,000 members with USD 2.2 billion in annualized revenue.
Top Holdings Performance
The company’s ten largest holdings, representing 75% of the portfolio, increased 2% in aggregate fair value during the quarter. The following table details the performance of each top-ten company.
Spring Health remained the largest holding at SEK 4.9 billion (22% of portfolio) with flat valuation, as the company scales toward USD 1 billion in annualized revenue while maintaining EBITDA profitability. Perk, the second-largest position at SEK 2.5 billion (11% of portfolio), increased 1% as it approaches USD 400 million in annualized revenue.
Enveda and Tandem Health delivered the strongest performance, with fair values rising 30% and 35% respectively following financing rounds priced above prior valuations. Tandem’s fundraising brought the company into the top ten for the first time.
However, three software holdings faced valuation pressure. Mews declined 6%, Pleo fell 15%, and Oviva dropped 13%, primarily because updated forward expectations held back multiples relative to peers. According to management commentary in the earnings call, these marks reflected calibration and peer movements rather than fundamental business deterioration, though Oviva was also affected by reimbursement changes in Germany.
Sector Performance Analysis
Performance varied significantly by investment sector during the quarter, as illustrated in the following sector-level waterfall chart.
Health & Bio holdings increased 4%, adding SEK 0.4 billion in value, largely driven by Enveda’s financing round. Emerging Companies rose 16%, contributing SEK 0.3 billion, led by Tandem Health’s entry into the top ten. These gains were partially offset by a 4% decline in Software holdings, which reduced value by SEK 0.2 billion due to Mews and Pleo marks, and a 2% decrease in Other Investments & Partnership Funds, which fell SEK 0.2 billion including climate tech write-downs.
The company’s portfolio companies demonstrated strong operational performance relative to public market peers, as shown in the following benchmarking analysis.
Both Health & Bio and Software portfolio companies achieved 32% revenue growth over the last twelve months, approximately 2-3 times faster than their respective peer groups. However, profitability metrics remain below mature public comparables, with Health & Bio posting a negative 2% EBITDA margin and Software showing a negative 12% margin, compared to peer group margins of 23% and 24% respectively. Management noted that the profitability gap is narrowing, with combined EBITDA margins improving 7 percentage points year-to-date.
Valuation Methodology and Currency Impact
Kinnevik’s valuation approach uses revenue and gross profit multiples derived from broad groups of listed peers for 82% of the private portfolio. The following analysis shows how peer multiple movements affected portfolio companies across different subsectors.
The quarter saw mixed peer development across subsectors. HealthTech peers rose 10%, providing support for Spring Health’s valuation despite the company being marked flat. However, Transactional SaaS peers fell 12%, contributing to declines at Pleo (down 20%) and within Navan (down 16%). Value-Based Care peers dropped 16%, though Cityblock’s valuation declined 22% partly due to dilution from the Homeward acquisition.
Currency exposure played a significant role in portfolio valuation, with 72% of the unlisted portfolio denominated in U.S. dollars and 25% in euros. The weakening Swedish krona contributed an estimated 3% uplift to portfolio value during the quarter.
Strategic Direction Under New Leadership
Chief Executive Officer Helena Saxon, who recently assumed the role, outlined three strategic priorities for the company going forward. The transformation plan centers on building a more focused portfolio around fewer, larger holdings in later growth stages where Kinnevik can add the most value as an owner. The company emphasized financial discipline, directing capital only to companies with clear paths to profitability while implementing rigorous cost management, including a target to reduce annual management costs to SEK 200 million by 2027.
Saxon stated during the presentation: "We will build a more focused portfolio and concentrate on fewer, larger profitable holdings in later growth stages where Kinnevik can be the best owner." This marks a strategic shift toward portfolio concentration and reduced complexity.
Market Reaction and Outlook
Despite the modest NAV gain and strong total shareholder return during the quarter, Kinnevik shares fell 6.01% in premarket trading following the presentation. The market reaction suggested investors remained concerned about valuation pressure from lower peer multiples in software, fintech and value-based care, as well as write-downs in climate tech holdings including Stegra being marked at zero.
The company did not provide traditional quarterly guidance but outlined specific portfolio company outlooks. Spring Health is scaling toward a USD 1 billion annualized revenue run rate while maintaining profitability. Perk is approaching USD 400 million in annualized revenue after 48% growth in 2025. Cityblock has reached approximately USD 2.2 billion in annualized revenue serving nearly 200,000 patients. Enveda is advancing three clinical programs in eczema, obesity and irritable bowel syndrome, while Tandem Health continues expanding its AI medical assistant across 14 European countries.
Management indicated the company will continue evaluating new investment opportunities but emphasized a selective approach focused on businesses with clear paths to profitability. Share buybacks remain a possible capital allocation tool but are not a priority during the current strategic transition.
Interim Chief Financial Officer Caspar Sjöstrand noted: "Our health and bio and software companies grew revenues by over 30%, including acquisitions. That is 2-3 times as fast as their broader listed peer groups." He acknowledged that profitability still lags but emphasized the gap is narrowing with combined EBITDA margins up 7 percentage points year-to-date.
The company’s strong balance sheet, with SEK 7.4 billion in net cash and a current ratio of 6.34, provides financial flexibility to execute the strategic transformation while navigating near-term valuation headwinds in certain portfolio subsectors.

data.title: Prodal startup Američanům, teď se veze na vlně padelu. Půlku jeho nové aplikace získává za miliony Miton
data.ai_summary: Investment group Miton is taking a 50% stake in padel app Ace, with founder Jiří Diblík leading development. Miton will invest millions, and the app, used by about 9,000 players, aims to expand into Europe. Diblík previously sold his mental health app VOS.health to Spring Health.
data.author: Ondřej Holzman
data.full_text:
Foto: Ace Jiří Diblík a Tomáš Hodboď vyvíjejí padelovou aplikaci Ace Sdílet Uložit 0 Baví vás články CzechCrunche? Vídejte je na Googlu častěji. Sledovat Upřednostnit Jiří Diblík už jednou svůj startup prodal do Ameriky, teď buduje další a znovu s investorem, který mu tehdy věřil jako první. Investiční skupina Miton se stává partnerem jeho padelové aplikace Ace a získává v ní poloviční podíl. Do projektu pošle řádově miliony korun, přesnou výši investice ani valuaci strany nezveřejnily. Partner Mitonu Tomáš Hodboď se do Ace zapojí naplno a má aplikaci dostat do zahraničí, osmadvacetiletý Diblík povede technickou a produktovou část. S Mitonem se Diblík potkává podruhé. Původem jablonecká investiční skupina byla v roce 2020 prvním investorem jeho aplikace pro duševní zdraví VOS.health, kterou vybudoval s Ondřejem Kopeckým a kterou podle zakladatelů využily přes čtyři miliony uživatelů. „Já do Ace přináším zkušenosti s budováním globálních B2C aplikací, Tomáš zkušenosti s budováním a škálováním úspěšných firem. S Mitonem mám skvělou zkušenost už z předchozího startupu,“ uvádí Diblík. VOS.health nakonec koupil newyorský jednorožec Spring Health, který má jako zákazníky spíše firmy, a tak po převzetí dvanáctičlenného českého týmu aplikaci pro běžné uživatele ukončil. Cena zveřejněná nebyla, podle zdrojů CzechCrunche šlo o jednotky milionů dolarů v hotovosti i akciích. „Někteří investoři na exitu vydělali, u jiných výsledek nenaplnil původní očekávání. Pro tým to ale dopadlo dobře,“ hodnotil Diblík prodej pro Forbes. Kopecký i většina týmu ve Spring Health v New Yorku pokračují, Diblík odešel po roce, ač měl vesting na tři roky. Dnes se věnuje vlastní skupině TBA (The Bold Apps) se spotřebitelskými aplikacemi. Hlavním tahounem je Lively, kterou založil s manželkou Bárou Diblíkovou, a celé portfolio má podle našeho červencového rozhovoru o životě po exitu přes deset milionů dolarů (přes 210 milionů korun) ročních opakovaných tržeb. Foto: Ace Česká padelová aplikace Ace Diblík, který se jako první Čech nechal kvůli podnikání zplnoletnit, tehdy říkal, že TBA si díky ziskovosti může dovolit růst bez externích peněz, strategického partnera ale nevylučoval. Ace, který do skupiny zařadil letos v únoru, je tak prvním projektem TBA, do něhož takového partnera pouští. Aplikace vznikla z Diblíkovy osobní potřeby. Padel sám aktivně hraje a na zápas jsou potřeba čtyři hráči podobné úrovně, které není vždy snadné najít. Aplikace Ace funguje jako vertikální sociální síť po vzoru Stravy pro běžce a cyklisty. Hráči v ní mají rating a historii zápasů a hledají soupeře či spoluhráče, místo aby se domlouvali přes WhatsApp. Podle Diblíka ji používá zhruba devět tisíc lidí, tedy víc než polovina z patnácti tisíc Čechů, kteří podle odhadů firmy hrají pravidelně. Součástí produktu se nově stane rezervační a klubový software FullClub, který Ace nabídne padelovým klubům zdarma. Kluby přes něj mohou spravovat kurty, turnaje, platby i komunitu bez licenčních poplatků. Nastartujte svou kariéru Více na CzechCrunch Jobs







Za aplikaci neplatí ani hráči a Diblík a spol. zatím neřeší, kdy a jak začne vydělávat. „Řešíme to, jak postavit sociální síť pro hráče, a věříme, že v budoucnu dokážeme zdroj peněz najít. Facebook v prvních letech taky zásadně neřešil, na čem bude vydělávat. Láme se to ve chvíli, kdy máte síť s milionem uživatelů, kterým dokážete zobrazovat reklamu. Když dokážete obsadit kurty, které by jinak byly volné, můžete jim i klubům nabízet prémiové funkce,“ vysvětluje pro Forbes Diblík. Byznysovou stránku teď přebírá Hodboď, který je partnerem Mitonu od roku 2013. Od roku 2006 budoval cenový srovnávač Heureka, v jehož čele stál do května 2013. S Michalem Jirákem spoluzaložil módní vyhledávač Glami, kde byl rovněž generálním ředitelem, a podílel se na růstu platformy Donio. „Padel roste rychleji, než mu kdokoliv stíhá stavět infrastrukturu. Chci dát Ace několik let svého času, aby se z něj stala aplikace číslo jedna pro hráče padelu,“ popisuje Hodboď. Další firmu, kterou by pomohl budovat, Hodboď hledal poslední roky poté, co opustil vedení Glami. Podle něj už dnes na rozjetí takového projektu není potřeba velký tým. Většinu práce na vývoji obstarali AI agenti, jak prozradil pro Forbes. „Doba je taková, že během vývoje už nemusíme živit tým dvaceti programátorů,“ vysvětluje Hodboď. Posledního půl roku na Ace pracovali jen oni dva bez dalších nákladů a teprve ve chvíli, kdy si ověřili, že model funguje, přibrali programátora, grafika a business development manažera. S takto malou sestavou se Ace chystá za hranice. Prorazit chce v Evropě, nejdřív v Polsku či na Slovensku a následně v německy mluvících zemích. Firma má ambici dosáhnout globálně milionu aktivních uživatelů. Největší platformou na trhu je přitom španělský Playtomic, který má mít zhruba půldruhého milionu aktivních uživatelů měsíčně. Sám vydělává hlavně na transakcích a softwaru pro kluby, zčásti i na mírných poplatcích od hráčů.

data.title: Spring Health Opens VERA-MH Harm-From-Others Safety Rubric for Public Comment
data.ai_summary: Spring Health expanded VERA-MH, an open-source AI safety benchmark for mental health, to include a harm-from-others safety rubric. The rubric evaluates AI responses to risk of physical or sexual violence across five areas, using 100 personas. Public feedback is open for 60 days ahead of Domestic Violence Awareness Month.
data.author: Spring Health

industries.name: Safety & Alignment Evaluation (red-teaming, harmful capability testing)

sic_codes.name: SERVICES-OFFICES & CLINICS OF DOCTORS OF MEDICINE

data.full_text: The expansion adds a harm-from-others safety area to VERA-MH, the first open-source AI safety benchmark for mental health, and invites public feedback ahead of Domestic Violence Awareness Month NEW YORK, Sept. 25, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Spring Health, a global mental health company built on one AI-native platform, today expanded VERA-MH, the first open-source AI safety benchmark for mental health, into a second clinical safety area: harm from others. As more people turn to AI for emotional support1, Spring Health is helping build the standards by which mental health AI should be measured. The VERA-MH Harm-From-Others rubric evaluates how AI systems respond when an adult describes being at risk of physical or sexual violence from another person. Developed with clinicians, subject-matter experts in interpersonal violence, and people with lived experience, it is scored across five areas: detecting the risk, confirming it, guiding the person to human care, supportive conversation, and following AI boundaries. Drawing on 100 realistic personas, it is the first open-source benchmark of its kind. "There are many moments when someone's safety depends on how an AI responds, and harm from others is one of the most urgent and least addressed," said Dr. Mill Brown, Chief Medical Officer at Spring Health. "In clinical care, we don't wait for a crisis to know what a safe response looks like. We train for it and hold ourselves to a standard. AI deserves that same rigor, not a guess." The expansion comes as VERA-MH gains independent validation. OpenAI's newly published MentalHealthBench paper cites VERA-MH's SI (suicidal ideation) rubric as one of the few frameworks built specifically to assess safe AI responses to risk. VERA-MH is open source, and any organization, including those building general-purpose AI models, can use it to test their own systems. It was launched in October 2025 in collaboration with members of the AI in Mental Health Safety and Ethics Council, including Dr. Nina Vasan of Stanford University School of Medicine, Lilly Wyttenbach of JPMorgan Chase, Dr. Don Mordecai of Kaiser Permanente, Hans Hage of UnitedHealthcare, Dr. Nils Opel of Charité – Berlin University Hospital, Dr. Julian De Freitas of Harvard Business School, Fred Thiele of Microsoft, Dr. Tim Hahn of the University of Münster, and Dr. John Krystal of Yale School of Medicine. In advance of Domestic Violence Awareness Month, public feedback on the Harm-From-Others rubric opens today for the next 60 days through an online form, the same process Spring Health used for the suicide-risk benchmark. The rubric and personas are published in the VERA-MH repository, which is open for feedback and contributions. About Spring Health Spring Health, is a global mental health company built on one AI-native platform so care follows individuals across every job, move, health plan, and life stage. In a 2025 OJPHI study, 92% of Spring Health members reliably improved or recovered from depression or anxiety. JAMA Network Open research found members recover 5.9 weeks faster than the leading competitor. Over two years, the Validation Institute found 21% net savings in mental health costs and 25% lower physical health spending versus matched controls. More than 170 million people worldwide have access to Spring Health through leading employers and health plans, including Highmark, Target, The Coca-Cola Company, BlackRock, Microsoft, Pfizer, and Wawa. Practice Innovations, 11(2), 139–155. https://doi.org/10.1037/pri0000292 SOURCE Spring Health

data.title: Six Organizations Honored for Shaping the First Decade of Workplace Mental Health Care
data.ai_summary: Spring Health named Adobe, BASF, Cincinnati Children's, Johnson & Johnson, Koch, and Nielsen as inaugural Pioneer Award recipients for advancing workplace mental health care. The six organizations cover over 536,000 lives and have made more than 90,000 lifetime appointments through Spring Health.
data.author: Spring Health

industries.name: Workplace Mental Health & EAP-Integrated Teletherapy Platforms

data.full_text: Spring Health's inaugural Pioneer Award honors Adobe, BASF, Cincinnati Children's Hospital Medical Center, Johnson & Johnson, Koch, and Nielsen for their leadership in advancing workplace mental health care NEW YORK, Sept. 22, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- In celebration of its tenth anniversary, Spring Health, a global mental health company built on one AI-native platform, named six organizations as the inaugural recipients of its Pioneer Award, honoring their leadership in advancing how employers deliver mental health benefits. At a time when workplace mental health care was still new and untested, Adobe, BASF, Cincinnati Children's, Johnson & Johnson, Koch, and Nielsen chose to invest early in a different way of caring for their people. HR and benefits leaders across these six organizations pushed for broader access, better outcomes for complex cases, and proof that the model could work at scale across a global workforce. Together, the six honorees represent more than 536,000 covered lives and over 90,000 lifetime appointments through Spring Health. "Being recognized as a Pioneer Award recipient highlights the investment in new technologies and better access to care that Koch has made for employees," said David Cheung, Senior Benefits Vendor Manager at Koch. "Our partnership with Spring Health has helped our members obtain timely, high-quality mental health resources in a format that fits their needs. We know that speed to care and therapeutic fit are vital pieces to helping people get better, faster." "Spring Health has been an essential partner in helping us reimagine what comprehensive workforce well‑being can look like in a healthcare environment," said Peter Adebi, Senior Vice President and Chief Human Resources Officer at Cincinnati Children's. "By co‑creating an integrated care model that includes on-site presence, we've expanded access, strengthened coordination, and supported our teams through some of their most challenging moments. The Pioneer Award reflects not only what we've achieved together, but what's possible when two organizations align around innovation, compassion, and long‑term impact." "Prioritizing employee well-being is at the core of who we are," said Kelly Hallac, Senior Director of Benefits & Wellbeing at Nielsen. "Through our partnership with Spring Health, we're proud to see high engagement and real clinical improvements in depression and anxiety, delivering meaningful, measurable support to our global workforce and their families." Across six different organizations, one thing holds constant: individual leaders who refused to accept mental health care as it was and pushed for something better on their employees' behalf. "These organizations helped us see where care still broke down for their people: the wait for a first appointment, the mismatch with a first provider, and no way to know whether it worked," said Gijo Mathew, Chief Product Officer at Spring Health. "We built Spring Health on AI from day one, so instead of explaining those gaps away, we fixed them: matching people to the right care faster, and finally proving whether it worked. Partnering on problems that hard is the standard these six set, and the one we still build against." Founded in 2016 by April Koh and Adam Chekroud, Spring Health has spent the past decade building a single platform that connects people to personalized care and measures whether it is working. In a 2025 OJPHI study of 52,929 members, 92% reliably improved or recovered from depression or anxiety. The Validation Institute has independently validated Spring Health's savings. Spring Health is the first mental health solution to guarantee net ROI, and every single customer has achieved it. The Pioneer Award recognizes the customers who helped turn Spring Health's ambitious mission to eliminate every barrier to mental health into measurable care. As Spring Health enters its second decade, it will keep building alongside customers, with the goal of care that stays continuous, personal, and effective as people's lives change. About Spring Health Spring Health is a global mental health company built on one AI-native platform so care follows individuals across every job, move, health plan, and life stage. In a 2025 OJPHI study, 92% of Spring Health members reliably improved or recovered from depression or anxiety. Over two years, the Validation Institute found 21% net savings in mental health costs and 25% lower physical health spending versus matched controls. data.title: Mental Health Apps Market to reach USD 29.20 Billion by 2035 at 14.0% CAGR
data.ai_summary: The global mental health apps market is projected to grow from USD 7.88 billion in 2025 to USD 29.20 billion by 2035, a 14.0% CAGR. Growth is driven by reimbursement pathways, employer purchasing, and conversational AI. North America holds 38.5% of 2025 revenue, while Asia-Pacific grows fastest at 17.2% CAGR.

data.full_text:
Mental Health Apps Market to reach USD 29.20 Billion by 2035 at 14.0% CAGR News Provided By Market Research Future Share This Article Mental Health Apps Market (2026 - 2035) Mental Health Apps Market to Surge from USD 7.88 Billion in 2025 to USD 29.20 Billion by 2035—By Reimbursement Finally Arriving, Employer Outcomes Purchasing NY, CA, UNITED STATES, September 17, 2026 /



The 14.0% CAGR is propelled by three converging forces: reimbursement pathways for digital therapeutics, with the U.S. Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services establishing payment pathways for FDA-cleared digital mental health treatment devices beginning January 2025 and Germany's DiGA directory listing prescription apps reimbursed at roughly EUR 200–500 per patient per quarter; employer behavioural benefit expansion, with roughly 77% of large U.S. employers flagging worsening workforce mental health and purchasing shifting from headcount-based EAP contracts to per-employee-per-month platform fees with utilisation and outcome guarantees; and conversational AI changing unit economics, with large language models cutting the marginal cost of a guided therapeutic conversation to near zero while structured AI-delivered CBT showed clinically meaningful symptom improvement in supervised settings.



Global regulatory and funding momentum is amplifying this shift. Behavioral health digital ventures absorbed roughly USD 2.7 billion in disclosed funding during 2024–2025, a share of overall digital health investment that has grown for four consecutive years. The National Health Service allocated approximately GBP 70 million toward digital therapeutics assessment and deployment through its Talking Therapies modernisation programme. North America holds 38.5% of 2025 revenue, anchored by employer-sponsored behavioural benefits and an unusually permissive reimbursement environment, while Asia-Pacific grows fastest at a 17.2% CAGR through 2035, propelled by India's Tele-MANAS rollout and China's National Mental Health Action Plan. Europe ranks second on share, where the German DiGA fast-track remains the world's most-copied prescription pathway.



Request A Free Sample:

https://www.marketresearchfuture.com/sample_request/19224



Key Market Trends & Growth Drivers



Reimbursement Finally Arrives



Payment, not product, was the binding constraint. CMS finalised HCPCS codes covering FDA-cleared digital mental health treatment devices with national payment amounts effective January 2025, and Germany's DiGA directory now lists prescription apps reimbursed at roughly EUR 200–500 per patient per quarter across statutory sickness funds. That converts a USD 60 annual consumer subscription into a several-hundred-dollar clinical episode. The revenue-per-user delta is the single most consequential economic change in the Mental Health Apps Market since app stores launched.



The Supply Side Cannot Scale



Employers Are Buying Outcomes



Large U.S. employers now report behavioural health as their top-cited benefit priority, with roughly 77% flagging worsening workforce mental health in recent benefits surveys. Purchasing has shifted from headcount-based EAP contracts to per-employee-per-month platform fees with utilisation and outcome guarantees. Vendors that publish depression symptom reduction data win those renewals, and employer and payer channels grow faster because they eliminate the monthly renewal decision.



Conversational AI Changes Unit Economics



Large language models cut the marginal cost of a guided therapeutic conversation to near zero, and 2024–2025 trial results for structured AI-delivered CBT showed clinically meaningful symptom improvement in supervised settings. Regulators have responded cautiously — several U.S. states passed statutes in 2025 restricting unsupervised AI therapy claims — but the cost curve is now permanently altered, and by 2030 most guided therapeutic interactions will be AI-mediated with human clinical oversight.

Market Segment Insights



BY PLATFORM



iOS: Largest segment with 38.0% share in 2025 , reflecting higher paid-conversion economics in North America and Western Europe. iOS leads revenue despite trailing Android on installed base, explained by subscriber willingness-to-pay in developed markets.



Android: Significant segment with 34.0% share in 2025 , driven by volume reach across Asia-Pacific and Africa.



Cross-platform/Hybrid: Significant segment with 21.0% share in 2025 , driven by enterprise deployment cost efficiency. Institutional contracts require device-agnostic coverage across an entire population.



Wearables-First: Fastest-growing platform at 19.4% CAGR (2026–2035) , driven by passive sleep and heart-rate-variability sensing. Bundling detection into devices consumers already wear removes the daily-open requirement that kills retention.



BY APPLICATION



Depression & Anxiety Management: Largest application at USD 2.64 Billion in 2025, driven by highest prevalence and reimbursement coverage. Captures the largest pool because it maps directly to reimbursable diagnostic codes.



Stress & Sleep Management: Significant segment at USD 1.89 Billion in 2025, driven by employer wellbeing programmes.



Meditation & Mindfulness Wellness: Significant segment at USD 1.54 Billion in 2025, driven by consumer subscription retention.



Substance Use & Addiction Recovery: Fastest-growing application at 15.8% CAGR (2026–2035) , driven by opioid settlement fund allocation. U.S. state opioid settlement disbursements have funded digital aftercare procurement at a pace few forecasters anticipated.



BY END USER



Homecare/Individuals: Largest segment with 52.0% share in 2025 , driven by direct-to-consumer subscription access. Individual consumers still account for the majority of spending, but their share is declining every year.



Employers & Payers: Fastest-growing end user with 24.0% share in 2025 , driven by benefit cost containment. Employer and payer channels grow faster because they eliminate the monthly renewal decision.



Providers & Clinics: Significant segment with 17.0% share in 2025 , driven by waiting-list step-care management.



Educational Institutions: Significant segment with 7.0% share in 2025 , driven by campus counselling capacity constraints.



BY AGE GROUP

data.title: AI Tools For Mental Health Are Proliferating Everywhere. Industry Leaders Are Rushing To Set Safety Standards.
data.ai_summary: APA Labs and Spring Health are developing safety standards for mental health AI tools, with APA's digital badge program and Spring's VERA-MH benchmark. The standards aim to prevent harm from unregulated chatbots, as 28% of adults 18-29 use them for mental health advice.
data.author: Rachel Curry

industries.name: Safety & Alignment Evaluation (red-teaming, harmful capability testing)

data.full_text: On the heels of Antropic researcher Jacob Coxon's highly publicized resignation from the company, in which the AI researcher said the largest companies in the sector are "gambling with our lives," one of the technology's use case remains chiefly unregulated, with particularly dire impacts when things go sideways. As 28% of adults ages 18–29 report they use major chatbots for mental health information or advice, the effort to set mental health AI standards is now ongoing. Tanya Carlson, managing director of APA Labs, a unit of the American Psychological Association, said "if a product fails, there can be really tragic consequences, so knowing what good looks like is really important." Beyond general purpose chatbots that, for many, double as mental health services, the market for purpose-built mental health AI tools have proliferated. APA Labs first introduced its digital badge program for mental and behavioral health technology in Aug. 2025 and expanded it the following April to include a publicly accessible library of independently reviewed tech that meets its criteria for safety and efficacy. Read more Trump Rejects Pacing AI Development, Takes On Anthropic's Amodei: 'Pretending To Be a 'Perfect Little Angel'' The World's Biggest AI Companies Were Racing To Build Faster. Now Their CEOs Are Hitting The Brakes. Sam Altman Joined Calls To Pace AI Development. He Says AI Could Get Out Of Control In Two Main Ways. Criteria for a digital badge includes: whether users are clearly informed about what the product is (and what it isn't), whether clinical or behavioral claims are supported by evidence, requires emergency contact info and more. "It has more than 400 criteria that we built with a group of experts and continue to revisit," said Carlson. Apps can receive either a bronze, silver or gold badge that reflects how closely they align with clinical criteria. Gold badge holders include wellbeing app Calm Health and conversational mental health support app Kai.ai. An anxiety brain training game called StarStarter holds a silver badge, for example. "We can see what happens when there's no consensus rubric," said Carlson. "Everybody's building their own thing, and the builders are going to lean into what they know, which means that you get products that may function right, but there isn't a deep knowledge of mental and behavioral health." For Carlson, most founders want to do better, which has made the digital badge program popular and caused APA Labs to expand their services to include CoLab, or a collaborative building option with expert insights from the ground up. APA Labs isn't the only organization working on standardizing mental health tech. Another organization, Spring Health—a platform that employers can offer to their workforce to connect with therapy and other mental health services—has built its own benchmark. Dubbed VERA-MH (validation of ethical and responsible AI in mental health), the company not only created a way to measure ethical AI in mental health chatbots, but it's using it to judge its own services, too. Launched in Oct. 2025, VERA-MH automatically conducts complete conversations with chatbots and scores responses based on five criteria (whether the chatbot detects risk, probes risk, takes appropriate actions, validates and collaborates with the user and maintains safe boundaries). When run against its own AI chatbot, Spring Health initially scored 76 out of 100 points. The gap, they found, was after recognizing a crisis, when they struggled to get a user person to a human clinician. "Once we knew that, we fixed it, and our score moved to 82," said Adam Chekroud, president of Spring Health. Chekroud added that the company open-sourced VERA-MH upon launch and ran it through a sixty-day public comment process before finalizing the rubric, ensuring the standard was shaped by outside scrutiny, too. "A bad recommendation from a shopping app is a bad experience," said Chekroud. "A bad response from a mental health AI, at the moment someone is in crisis, can contribute to serious harm, as alleged in wrongful-death lawsuits and discussed in congressional testimony." First filed in Aug. 2025, Raine v. OpenAI is an ongoing wrongful death lawsuit over the death of Adam Raine, a 16-year-old who completed suicide after OpenAI allegedly encouraged his suicidal ideation. In Sept. 2025, the U.S. Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism held a hearing examining the harm of AI chatbots, with Dr. Mitch Prinstein, then-chief of psychology at the APA, testifying that chatbots worsen overall mental health and increase loneliness. Regarding other frameworks for analyzing mental health AI tools, Carlson said, "The more smart people that are looking at a problem, the better, especially in a space that's as dynamic and critical as digital mental and behavioral health." For Chekroud, the important thing is that a developer isn't "grading its own homework." Granted, Spring Health analyzed its AI chatbot with its own VERA-MH, but the outside scrutiny that helped shape the tool lessens the bias. Plus, he added, "When we went looking for an external benchmark to check our own work against, there wasn't one." Because AI relies on natural language to communicate, general-purpose chatbots innately blur the lines between causal conversation and mental health support. However, as new benchmarks emerge for specialized tools—and perhaps for broader AI tools in the future—the industry is moving towards a more accountable future. Most people inside these companies want to build responsibly," said Chekroud. "Wanting to and being checked by someone outside the building are different things."

data.title: 5 Behavioral Health VC Investors to Watch
data.ai_summary: VC funding in behavioral health rebounded in 2026 after a 2024 low, with large rounds like Talkiatry's $210M Series D and Grow Therapy's $150M Series D. The article highlights five firms—GreyMatter, Goldman Sachs Alternatives, Kaiser, General Catalyst, and HealthQuest—backing tech-enabled providers and specialized services.
data.author: Ashleigh Hollowell
data.full_text:
This is an exclusive BHB+ story.

Venture capital investments in behavioral health are emerging from a lull as firms recalibrated their priorities in 2024 and have since identified new strategic targets as the sector has matured.

Behavioral health, and in particular digital mental health solutions, saw an influx of capital in 2021, driven by the pandemic, with funding peaking around $4.9 billion, according to Rock Health. After that, there was talk of VC capital “drying up” around early 2022. Since then, VC funding dipped to a low of $1.4 billion in 2024. But behavioral health venture capital funding has recently been reinvigorated by investor conviction, a wave of new mental health startups and large growth funding rounds that target specialized, high-acuity services.

VC investments in behavioral health began the year with large capital rounds paid to platforms that target access and infrastructure, including a $210 million Series D round for Talkiatry, a $150 million Series D round for Grow Therapy, $80 million out of stealth for Salma Health and $40 million for AnswerNow’s telehealth applied behavioral analysis (ABA) services. All four of those mega fundraises took place during the first quarter of 2026.

Advertisement

VC investments across behavioral health during the second quarter of 2026 looked a bit different, with more attention to specialty services and slightly smaller, though still noteworthy, capital raises, including deals like Click Therapeutics’ $50 million Series D and a $30 million round for Instride Health.

Now that the market has matured past the COVID-induced telehealth arms race, venture capital funding is being prioritized for providers and solutions that have promising infrastructure and aim to improve access rather than merely investing in the promise of digital mental health.

Across all five VC firms that Behavioral Health Business is watching, one theme is clear: behavioral health is embracing technology, and the future belongs to strategic providers with scalable, tech-enabled, payer-aligned care models.

Talkiatry

TownHome Health

Valera Health

Vanna Health

Willow Health

Why BHB is watching:

San Francisco-based GreyMatter Capital is a venture firm that invests solely in mental health founders. It has a swath of behavioral health providers and tech-enabled solutions in its investment portfolio, but a handful have raised significant capital to scale in the last year.

In February, virtual psychiatry provider Talkiatry raised a $210 million Series D round, which was almost the total of all the funding it had received up to that point, bringing its total funding to roughly $452 million. The company will use much of the new funding to bolster its AI capabilities.

Another one of GreyMatter’s portfolio companies, pediatric psychiatric care provider Flourish Health, raised $26 million for its Series A round in July. Its goal is to scale high-acuity psychiatric care for youth populations.

Serious mental illness provider Vanna Health secured $17 million in a Series B round earlier this summer and will use the capital to enter new markets soon. The company also named a new CEO shortly before the fundraise. One of the new CEO’s goals is to deepen payer partnerships and wraparound services for patients.

Pediatric speech, occupational and physical therapy provider Coral Care, another GreyMatter investment, secured a $13 million Series A in February, and aims to connect families with therapists for in-home services. The company noted that with this funding, it will move to scale nationally.

Other noteworthy developments among GreyMatter’s portfolio companies this year include the acquisition of Valera Health by Mindoula in July. Terms of the deal were not disclosed, but Mindoula noted the deal was a move to expand its collaborative care model with established psychiatric services.

Another one we’re watching in this portfolio is Pelago’s announcement that it will transition from being historically a substance use disorder (SUD) care provider and expand into general behavioral health. Its first move in this vein was a wellness support chatbot capable of escalating issues to Pelago’s in-house clinical team.

Goldman Sachs Alternatives Growth Equity

Noteworthy behavioral health investments:

Grow Therapy

Why BHB is watching:

Goldman Sachs Alternatives Growth Equity’s portfolio company Grow Therapy made headlines earlier this year when it secured a whopping $150 million Series D round in March 2026. That brought the digital mental health platform’s projected annual revenue to more than $1 billion. Prior to the large capital round, Grow Therapy made a strategic investment and acquired the AI scribe tool Tenor Therapy in February. The company’s last funding round prior to its Series D was an $88 million Series C in 2024. The new infusion of capital, coupled with its latest acquisition, positions it to make additional, scalable investments going forward in the sector.

Kaiser Permanente Ventures

Noteworthy behavioral health investments:

Headspace

Groups Recover Together

Mind 24-7

Noto (formerly NOCD)

Why BHB is watching:

Kaiser Permanente Ventures made BHB’s list of VC firms to watch in 2025, as well, but for different reasons. This year, the firm’s portfolio companies Headspace, Groups Recover Together and NOCD all were part of significant, strategic transactions.

Virtual mental health provider Headspace is set to be acquired by Sword Health in a cash deal reportedly valued at $300 million. The valuation is lower than some in the industry expected, particularly as many have had Headspace on their bingo cards as a company that could potentially IPO. The transaction comes just about one year after Headspace launched its direct-to-consumer therapy services. Sword Health, a New York City-based digital health provider, began making moves into behavioral health last summer and its valuation jumped to $4 billion. Sword Health’s CEO Virgilio Bento previously told HB that expanding capabilities into SMI care and growing its AI offerings, are part of its trajectory on its path toward a possible 2028 IPO.

Addiction treatment provider Groups Recover Together, another investment in Kaiser’s portfolio, made its first-ever acquisition in March 2026 and hinted that more activity in that vein is likely on the horizon. Its purchase of Better Life Partners deepens its resources throughout New England and introduces new care model elements that will allow the company to expand into new territories. Better Life Partners had been a bit of a distressed asset, with a series of financial and operational issues. Still, it had two assets that Groups wanted: virtual responsive care and walk-in clinic capabilities, CEO Cooper Zelnick, told BHB. Those are likely to scale further across the company over time.

Virtual OCD provider NOCD, another one of Kaiser’s portfolio companies, acquired trauma care provider Rebound Health earlier this year. Now the two entities operate under the new brand identity “Noto.” The transaction follows a market trend BHB has been keeping tabs on, where several new providers entering the market are entering niche areas of care and adding on, rather than starting broad and trying to narrow. The deal added trauma-focused care capabilities, which NOCD did not previously provide. An ongoing priority now for the newly formed company Noto is to continue to add new services for other complex behavioral health conditions.

General Catalyst

Noteworthy behavioral health investments:

Radial

Birches Health

Ophelia Health

Cortica

Elemy

Cartwheel Care

Eleanor Health

Equip Health

InStride Health

Osmind

Rippl

SonderMind

Spring Health

Why BHB is watching:

General Catalyst has long been a powerhouse investment firm known for backing successful healthcare companies with venture investments. Throughout 2026, several of its portfolio companies were part of sizable transactions or on the receiving end of large capital infusions.

Late last year, General Catalyst led a $50 million funding round for New York City-based Radial, which provides clinic-based interventional psychiatry services like transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), Spravato, and neuromodulation treatments. Not only was the funding a vote of confidence from its investors, zooming out, interventional psychiatry is also on the rise across the industry as the latest hot commodity.

Following the $50 million Series A round, Radial acquired Mindful Health Solutions, a larger and older outpatient operator, this August for an undisclosed amount. Mindful Health Solutions has similar interventional psychiatry offerings and this single deal exponentially multiplied Radial’s geographic footprint. Radial is less than one year into its hold period with General Catalyst and anticipates tailwinds from the boom in interventional psychiatry will propel it further.

Also, as part of General Catalyst’s massive investment portfolio, Spring Health disclosed its plans to acquire digital mental health platform Alma in January. The transaction took place amid a wave of digital health dealmaking that began in 2026. Digital mental health is an area that is likely to continue to see consolidation following the explosion of solutions out of the pandemic, which is starting to balance out. Spring’s move to buy Alma skyrocketed its revenue expectations to $1 billion in its first year following the close of the deal, with its valuation rising to between $6 billion and $7 billion.

Other noteworthy developments among General Catalyst’s investments this year were also InStride Health’s $30 million Series C and Birches Health’s $20 million capital raise. Pediatric behavioral health provider InStride raised the capital at the beginning of 2026 and told BHB it plans to use it to expand into new markets. Birches Health’s funding came late in 2025, but has remained noteworthy in 2026, as both public and private audiences have renewed their attention on gambling addiction, which is one of its primary service lines. It’s likely there will be more expansion or consolidation in this area of behavioral and process addictions over time as concerns about gambling and social media rise.

HealthQuest Capital

Noteworthy behavioral health investments:

AnswersNow

Why BHB is watching:

Virtual autism therapy provider AnswersNow secured a $40 million Series B in January, marking its first fundraise since 2023. The company provides ABA care via telehealth with board-certified behavior analysts (BCBAs), which is typically a clinic-based service. AnswersNow executives said that following the new capital infusion, its focus will be on “aggressively” scaling its platform, eventually adding new service lines and expanding its use of AI. HealthQuest Capital successfully exited AmWell, another behavioral health company, in the past.

data.title: Barriers to mental health care look different across your workforce
data.ai_summary: Spring Health surveyed 1,500+ employees across five countries on mental health care barriers, finding cost and time as top obstacles. Lower-income workers cited cost, while higher-income workers cited privacy concerns, and awareness of benefits varied by income. The report urges employers to design support around these differing barriers.
data.author: Hayden Goethe For Spring Health
data.full_text:

Employers may offer benefits. Leaders may say the right things. But when someone actually needs care, the real barriers to mental health tend to be practical:
And those barriers are not the same for everyone.
As part of research for its 2026 Workplace Mental Health Annual Report, Spring Health surveyed 1,500+ full-time employees across five different countries (the United States, Canada, Mexico, India, and the United Kingdom). Employees pointed to a familiar set of obstacles to accessing care.
And while the overall group surveyed clearly identified their top barriers, the leading barriers are more nuanced when age, income, and other factors are considered.
When employees are asked what gets in the way of mental health support, the answers are strikingly practical.
Across Spring Health’s research, employees said the top barriers are:
That matters because when support is hard to find, hard to trust, or hard to use, the benefit may exist on paper without making a real difference in people’s lives.
Income levels significantly influenced responses to top barriers to care. While Spring Health’s research was global, U.S. respondents were asked for their household income levels (within a range of options). Information about income-influenced barriers was compelling.
Among U.S. respondents, for lower-income employees, cost was the defining barrier. Slowly, as you moved to higher income brackets within the research, lack of time became the prevailing barrier.
Privacy concerns is another important nuance. Just 16% of employees with household incomes less than $25,000 cited privacy concerns, compared with 37% of those with household incomes of over $150,000.
That suggests that more senior or highly compensated employees may need something more than broad reassurance. They may need concrete proof that using mental health support is confidential, discreet, and safe.
Before employees can use a benefit, they have to know it exists.
Spring Health research also shows that awareness of employer-sponsored mental health benefits tracks strongly with income. Among employees with household incomes under $50,000, just 47% said their employer offers mental health benefits. Among employees with household incomes of at least $150,000, 80% said their employer offers mental or behavioral health benefits.
The report also found that 34% of employees say they are either not offered mental health benefits or are unsure whether they are, which indicates the possibility that many employees are simply unaware of the care available to them. For example, according to Mental Health America, 98% of mid-to-large U.S. companies offer an Employee Assistance Program (EAP).
For lower-income employees especially, the barrier may begin even earlier than cost or wait times. If the benefit is poorly explained, rarely mentioned, or buried in HR materials, access breaks down before care becomes a possibility.
Among global employees ages 18-34, the top barriers were:
However, as populations within the survey got older, cost emerged as the top concern. But the percentage impacted by cost didn’t change much due to age; it’s simply that lack of time and availability declined as barriers.
Among employees 55 years of age and older, the top barriers were:
Younger employees may face more time pressure at work, or feel less able to make time for care. Older employees may still face affordability challenges.
Mental health equity requires recognizing that employees do not all start from the same place. There’s a distinction between equality and equity. Equity means recognizing that barriers differ across circumstances and ensuring people receive support that reflects those realities.
For one employee, the barrier is cost. For another, it is the fear that seeking support will not stay private. For another, it is not being able to take a call during the workday. For another, it is long wait times for therapy. For another, it is not knowing whether the employer offers anything at all.
That is why removing barriers to mental health services has to go beyond awareness campaigns or one open enrollment mention per year. The support itself has to be easier to start.
If employers want to improve access to mental health care, they need to design around the barriers employees actually face.

data.title: Mental health utilization is up - but employer spending fell 7% in 2025
data.ai_summary: In 2025, 73% of large employers reported increased mental health and substance use disorder utilization, while average employer spending fell about 7% year over year. The gap between rising demand and falling investment is widening, and brokers are advised to evaluate network connectivity and outcomes data at renewal.
data.author: Mark Rosanes

industries.name: Behavioral Health Provider Network Management & Credentialing
Large Group Health Insurance (Mid-Market & National Accounts)

data.full_text:
The gap between rising demand and falling investment is widening, and brokers have a clear role at renewal Benefits By Mark Rosanes Aug 31, 2026 Share Seventy-three percent of large employers reported increased utilization of mental health and substance use disorder services in 2025, and another 17% expected demand to climb further, according to the Business Group on Health's 2026 Employer Health Care Strategy Survey. The problem for brokers helping clients navigate renewal is that employer spending on mental health resources moved in the opposite direction: NFP's 2026 US Benefits Trend Report found average spending fell roughly 7% year over year in 2025. That gap - rising demand, falling investment - is the central tension in employer mental health benefits right now, and it is shaping both the vendor landscape and the conversations brokers need to be having with clients before next renewal. Why access remains the core problem The treatment gap in the US sits in the background of every employer mental health conversation. SAMHSA's 2024 National Survey on Drug Use and Health found that 61.5 million adults - 23.4% of the US population - had any mental illness in 2024, but only about 52% received treatment. That leaves roughly 29.5 million adults with a diagnosable condition who received no care. Insurance coverage is a significant factor in whether people access care. Platforms built around insurance reimbursement - Grow Therapy, Headway, and Talkiatry - have scaled most rapidly by reducing the friction between a patient's coverage and an available in-network provider. Grow Therapy reported facilitating 7 million visits in 2025, raised a $150 million Series D in March at a $3 billion valuation, and stated coverage of 220 million insured Americans through partnerships with more than 125 health plans. That model - insurance-first, provider network at scale - is increasingly where the employer market is heading. The EAP model's structural limits The traditional employee assistance program (EAP) is where most employers currently anchor their mental health benefit, and utilization data suggests it is underperforming. A Prudential Group Insurance survey, cited in an August 2025 report, found that while 59% of employers offer EAPs, more than half of eligible employees have never used one. Barriers include concerns about confidentiality, uncertainty about what the program covers, and stigma. Industry estimates typically put annual EAP utilization at between 3% and 6% of eligible employees, though rates vary by employer size and program design. Low utilization conceals a downstream cost that brokers can make visible. An employee who does not use an EAP and whose mental health needs escalate will often surface in the claims data later through higher short-term disability costs, increased absenteeism, or more intensive health plan utilization. Brokers who can show employer clients the cost of untreated mental health conditions using their own claims data have a more concrete case for upgrading the benefit than engagement metrics alone provide. The shift in the vendor landscape reflects this pressure. Platforms like Lyra Health, Spring Health, and Modern Health have replaced or augmented traditional EAPs at a growing share of mid-market and enterprise employers, offering faster matching, more sessions, and measurable outcomes reporting. Spring Health reports engagement rates often ten times the traditional EAP average. What brokers need to evaluate at renewal Two structural questions now define the employer mental health benefit conversation at renewal. The first is whether the current offering connects to the health plan's behavioral health network, or runs beside it. An EAP that operates parallel to the health plan but does not hand off to in-network providers creates an access cliff - employees exhaust EAP sessions and then face the full barrier of finding in-network care on their own. Universal Health Services' $835 million acquisition of Talkspace, completed August 17, is a direct market response to that structural gap. It creates a referral pathway from virtual therapy through to inpatient behavioral health within a single organization, removing a coordination step that brokers and EAP administrators have typically had to handle manually. The second question is whether the employer can measure what the benefit is producing. Business Group on Health noted that with utilization rates now high, employers should shift focus from access to unit cost and quality, specifically whether employees are getting the right mental health support at the right time. More than half of eligible employees have never used their EAP, and the vendors gaining ground in 2026 are those providing employers with outcomes data rather than session counts alone. The employer mental health benefit is no longer a renewal checkbox. The data on rising utilization, falling investment, and a widening access gap creates a clear advisory opening. Audit what the client has, determine whether it connects to the health plan network, assess whether outcomes data is available, and use claims data to make the cost-of-inaction case. Employer health costs are on a 15-year high trajectory, and mental health utilization is now explicitly identified as a cost driver alongside GLP-1s and specialty drugs. Brokers who can frame the evaluation clearly for clients are better positioned heading into a difficult renewal environment. data.title: Weekly Buzz: RARE, REGN Secure FDA Nod, BMRN Stikes Deal; HUMA, EYPT Face Trial Setbacks
data.ai_summary: The biopharma sector saw significant regulatory and strategic activity, highlighted by FDA approvals for Ultragenyx's GENGLYCOS, Regeneron's Pasatru, and Implantica's RefluxStop, alongside a $490 million acquisition of Alesta Therapeutics by BioMarin. Clinical developments included positive Phase 3 results for argenx in autoimmune myositis and Merck/Moderna in melanoma, contrasted with setbacks for EyePoint's wet AMD trial and AstraZeneca's lung cancer study.
data.full_text:
This week's global biopharma roundup captured a mix of regulatory approvals, strategic partnerships, acquisitions, and merger activity, alongside clinical trial breakthroughs and halts. Positive readouts across autoimmune myositis, glioma, and melanoma were offset by setbacks in wetAMD and lung cancer, underscoring the sector volatility.

Let's take a closer look at the details.

FDA Approvals

FDA Approves Ultragenyx's GENGLYCOS, First-Ever Treatment for GSDIa

Ultragenyx Pharmaceutical Inc. (RARE), announced that the FDA has granted accelerated approval for GENGLYCOS (DTX401) in adult and pediatric patients with glycogen storage disease type Ia (GSDIa). The therapy, delivered via AAV8 gene transfer, is the FDA-apporved treatment addressing the root cause of this ultra-rare genetic disorder, reducing reliance on burdensome cornstarch regimens and lowering risk of severe hypoglycemia.

RARE closed Thursday's trading (August 20, 2026) at $25.32, down 3.51%

Implantica Wins FDA Nod for RefluxStop

Implantica AG (8IM1.F) secured U.S. FDA Premarket Approval for RefluxStop, its implant-based therapy for gastroesophageal reflux disease. The approval, backed by five-year safety and efficacy data, paves the way for a U.S. commercial launch following use in nearly 1,800 patients across Europe.

Implantica closed Thursday's trading at $4.84

Regeneron Wins FDA Approval for Pasatru in FOP

Regeneron Pharmaceuticals, Inc. (REGN), announced that the FDA has approved Pasatru (garetosmab-grts) to reduce new heterotopic ossification lesions and flare-ups in adults with fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP). Backed by Phase 3 data showing up to 94% reduction in new lesions, the approval marks a breakthrough for patients with this ultra-rare disorder.

REGN closed Thursday's trading at $826.64, down 1.69%

Lupin Gets FDA Nod for Generic Wakix

Lupin Ltd. (LUPIN) announced that the FDA has approved its Abbreviated New Drug Application for Pitolisant Tablets, 4.45 mg and 17.8 mg, as bioequivalent to Harmony Biosciences' Wakix for narcolepsy indications. The approval expands Lupin's sleep disorder portfolio and positions the company to compete in a growing U.S. market.

For the full year 2025, Harmony Biosciences' narcolepsy drug Wakix's net revenue increased to $868.45 million from $714.73 million in the prior year. Looking ahead Wakix net revenue is expected to be in the range of $1.0-$1.04 billion in FY 2026.

LUPIN closed Friday's trading at INR 2,201, up 0.01%

Deals

IDEAYA Biosciences Signs Clinical Collaboration With Genentech On Pancreatic Cancer Study

IDEAYA Biosciences, Inc. (IDYA) signed a clinical collaboration with Genentech, a member of the Roche Group, to evaluate the efficacy and safety of IDE892, its investigational MTA-cooperative PRMT5 inhibitor, in combination with Genentech's GDC-7035, a KRAS G12D inhibitor, in patients with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.

As per the agreement, Genentech will sponsor the clinical combination study, and IDEAYA will supply IDE892. Also, both companies will each retain all commercial rights to their respective compounds, including as monotherapy and as combination therapies.

IDYA closed Thursday's trade at $39.11, up 0.62%.

Spring Health Pairs with Alight Partner Network to Expand Mental Health Access

Alight, Inc. (ALIT) unveiled a strategic partnership with Spring Health, a mental health company built on an AI-native platform, to join the Alight Partner Network, which offers solutions designed to help employers deliver a more connected and engaging employee experience.

The collaboration is designed to surface mental health support earlier by integrating Spring Health into the Alight Worklife platform, which generates more than 210 million annual interactions across health, wealth and leave programs. Through Spring Health, employees can access mental health support from self-guided tools and coaching to therapy, medication management, and crisis care.

ALIT closed Thursday's trade at $13.41, up 2.61%.

BioMarin Acquires Alesta in Deal Worth Up to $490 Mln

BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc. (BMRN) has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Alesta Therapeutics, securing rights to its lead clinical-stage candidate ALE1, which is in a phase 1/2a trial for hypophosphatasia (HPP), a rare genetic bone disease.

Under the terms of the deal, BioMarin will pay $275 million upfront, with an additional $215 million in milestone payments tied to development and regulatory achievements. Alesta will spin out all non-ALE1 assets into a new entity before closing, and employees will transfer to the spinout. The transaction is expected to be completed this quarter.

BMRN closed Thursday's trade at $67.68, down 2.38%.

Trinity Biotech's Trinovium Partners With Echelon For AI Data Center Cooling Solutions

Trinity Biotech (TRIB), through its Trinovium subsidiary, has partnered with Echelon Data Centres to develop liquid cooling solutions for AI and high-density computing. The collaboration will focus on direct-to-chip cooling fluids, thermal management systems, and modular cooling technologies for next-generation data centres.

The move targets the rapidly growing data centre liquid cooling market, which is projected to expand from about $4 billion in 2026 to $27 billion by 2033, driven by AI workloads and higher data centre power densities.

TRIB closed Thursday's trade at $10.55, down 4.18%.

Fulcrum and Slate Enter Merger Deal

Fulcrum Therapeutics, Inc. (FULC) and Slate Medicines, Inc. announced that they have entered into a definitive all-stock merger agreement to form a combined company focused on next-generation migraine therapies that will operate under the name Slate Medicines, Inc. and trade on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol SLTE.

Under the terms of the merger, pre-merger Fulcrum stockholders are expected to own 5.0% of the combined company while Slate stockholders will own 95%. Fulcrum will contribute about $20.3 million in net cash and pay a cash dividend of an estimated $270 million to its stockholders immediately prior to closing expected in the fourth quarter of 2026.

FULC closed Thursday's trade at $3.85, up 1.53%.

Skye To Acquire Redx Pharma

Skye Bioscience, Inc (SKYE) and Redx Pharma Ltd. entered into a definitive transaction agreement under which Skye will acquire Redx through a scheme of arrangement and the combined company will be led by Redx's current management board and will operate under the name Fibrx Therapeutics, Inc.

The transaction is backed by approximately $125 million in gross financing for the combined company to fund operations and advance the lead program, RXC008, in a Phase 2 clinical trial for fibrostenotic Crohn's disease. The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter of 2026.

SKYE closed Thursday's trade at $0.28, down 8.34%.

Clinical Trials - Breakthroughs & Setbacks

Humacyte's Bioengineered Vessel Shows Positive One-Year Data in Phase 3 Hemodialysis Access Trial

Humacyte, Inc. (HUMA), a biotechnology company, announced the publication of one-year results from its V007 Phase 3 clinical trial evaluating its acellular tissue-engineered vessel (ATEV) for arteriovenous (AV) access in patients requiring hemodialysis in The Lancet Digital Health.

According to the company, in a trial comparing ATEV with the standard autogenous arteriovenous fistula (AVF), a surgical connection commonly used for dialysis access, ATEV provided superior outcomes after one year, particularly in patient groups at higher risk of fistula failure, including all women and men with obesity and diabetes.

HUMA closed Thursday's trade at $0.68, down 7.28%.

Merck, Moderna Phase 3 Combo Shows Survival Benefits In Melanoma

Merck (MRK) and Moderna, Inc. (MRNA)'s Phase 3 INTerpath-001 trial evaluating Intismeran autogene (V940/mRNA-4157), an investigational mRNA-based individualised neoantigen therapy, in combination with KEYTRUDA (pembrolizumab) for patients with completely resected stage IIB-IV melanoma met its primary endpoint of recurrence-free survival (RFS) and a key secondary endpoint of distant metastasis-free survival (DMFS).

Notably, the combo demonstrated statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvements in RFS and DMFS compared with KEYTRUDA alone, the current standard of care, with safety profiles consistent with earlier studies and no new safety signals according to the company.

MRK closed Thursday's trade at $148.99, down 2.11%.

MRNA closed Thursday's trade at $133.32, down 0.44%.

NeOnc's NEO100 Outperforms Historical Benchmark in Phase 2a Glioma Trial

NeOnc Technologies Holdings Inc. (NTHI) reported positive Phase 2a results for its investigational intranasal NEO100 in recurrent IDH1-mutant high-grade glioma, demonstrating a 48.9% six-month progression-free survival rate versus a 20% historical benchmark, with a median overall survival of approximately 26 months.

According to the company, NEO100 achieved a PFS rate 2.5 times the historical benchmark with no major toxicities. Median overall survival was approximately 26 months, with roughly 87% of patients alive at six months, 61% at one year, and 54% at two years. NeOnc now plans to meet with the FDA to discuss the path toward a larger registrational study.

NTHI closed Thursday's trade at $4.56, down 1.51%.

EyePoint's DURAVYU Phase 3 LUGANO Trial Misses Key Goal

EyePoint, Inc. (EYPT) reported that LUGANO, the first of two pivotal Phase 3 trials evaluating DURAVYU for wet age-related macular degeneration (wet AMD), failed to meet the primary endpoint of change from baseline in best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA), despite outperforming on key secondary endpoints.

Based on the outcomes across key secondary endpoints, paired with visual improvement, the company remains on track to report topline data from the second wet AMD pivotal Phase 3 LUCIA trial in the fourth quarter of 2026. The company anticipates filing an NDA for DURAVYU to treat wet AMD in the first half of 2027.

EYPT closed Thursday's trade at $5.46, down 14.29%.

AstraZeneca Halts Phase 3 EVOLVE-Lung02 Trial

AstraZeneca PLC (AZN) halted the Phase 3 eVOLVE-Lung02 trial evaluating Volrustomig, a dual-checkpoint bispecific antibody plus chemotherapy, after an Independent Data Monitoring Committee (IDMC) review concluded the combo was unlikely to achieve its dual primary endpoints in first-line metastatic non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC).

Meanwhile, AstraZeneca said the other Phase 3 trials of volrustomig in cervical cancer, head and neck squamous cell carcinoma and mesothelioma will continue as planned.

AZN closed Thursday's trade at $164.49, down 0.28%.

argenx Reports Positive Phase 3 Results In Autoimmune Myositis

argenx SE (ARGX) announced that its Phase 3 ALKIVIA trial of VYVGART Hytrulo in adults with autoimmune myositis met its primary endpoint, showing a statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvement in disease activity at Week 52. The therapy was well-tolerated, with a safety profile consistent with prior studies, according to the company.

VYVGART Hytrulo is already approved in generalised myasthenia gravis and is being studied across multiple autoimmune diseases.

ARGX closed Thursday's trade at $1038.12, up 0.51%

For more biotech stock news, visit rttnews.com.

data.title: How Is Your EAP Being Used?
data.ai_summary: The article contrasts Employee Assistance Program (EAP) utilization trends, noting that U.S. referrals are dominated by mental health counseling while Latin American firms like First Factory see significant usage of legal and financial services. This divergence is attributed to regional economic pressures, such as currency fluctuations in Costa Rica reducing purchasing power, alongside broader workplace anxieties driven by AI fears and inflation.
data.author: Don Gregori
data.full_text:
Data suggests that employees in U.S. and Latin American countries rely more on different services.

In the United States, mental health counseling makes up 79 percent of Employee Assistance Program referrals, according to one EAP provider’s internal data. That share rose from 71 percent just a year earlier. The story most people tell about EAPs, that they’re mainly a counseling benefit with a few extras attached, holds up against that number.

While comprehensive EAP utilization data is scarce, my company’s 2025 utilization data tells a different story. First Factory is a nearshore software consulting and development firm with a predominantly Latin America-based workforce. Our data show that psychological consultations make up 51 percent of cases, legal consultations are 32 percent, and financial consultations are 11 percent. Nutrition rounds out the rest. Half the utilization is something other than mental health counseling. This usage may come as a surprise, but there is good reasoning behind the needs. EAP background An Employee Assistance Program is an employer-provided benefit that offers confidential support services. Most programs cover a set number of sessions across a few categories: counseling, legal referrals, financial guidance, and general work-life support. Counseling is the category everyone expects. Legal and financial are categories most people don’t.

EAPs are no longer a rare perk. In 2024, 82 percent of U.S. employers offered one, according to SHRM. Providers typically price these programs per employee per month, generally $1 to $5 depending on geography and scope. National utilization statistics are hard to nail down, but estimates target 6.5 percent in 2019. Trends outside the U.S. Latin America-focused EAP providers highlight more than mental health services as core pillars of their service. A rising middle class, greater employment with global companies, and emerging laws all contribute to the need and focus.

Currency matters here too. Costa Rica’s colón has strengthened sharply against the U.S. dollar since 2022. For workers whose income is set in dollars, which is many in the country, that’s a real impact on an employee’s net pay. Add that to the rising costs of goods and services and the increase in turnover rates working for North American companies, and employees are feeling the pinch, both emotionally and financially. The rate of exchange in June 2022 was around 685 colóns per dollar, whereas today it is more than 200 points lower. That is about a 30 percent decline in purchasing power. Financial counseling under the EAP often begins by discussing saving strategies for a family and retirement, but can often turn into a real estate conversation. This shifts the financial planning conversation into a legal one. The global trade dynamics and currency swings that Americans gloss over are highly personal, specific problems for people whose pay or savings sit on the wrong side of the exchange rate. Work is less stable, net pay in one’s country’s currency is reduced, and the cost of everything is much higher than in previous years. It’s no wonder that EAP utilization statistics are up, and there’s a shift to leveraging more of the financial and legal services offered. For companies with a distributed global workforce, it’s important to dig deeper into each region’s behaviors and unique needs.

In the U.S., that share has been climbing fast. Most specifically, emotional concerns more than doubled between 2023 and 2024, from 8 percent to 18 percent, per one EAP’s data. Four things are driving that increase according to a recent Modern Health workplace report:

1. AI is now a named source of workplace anxiety, not a background worry. Sixty-nine percent of employees believe AI will lead to layoffs at their company within three years. Forty-nine percent fear losing their own job to AI. 2. Financial pressure has broadened past the usual budget conversation. Seventy percent of workers report increased financial stress tied to inflation and market volatility. More are worried about the broader economic impact of tariffs on their own household. 3. Political and social strain isn’t staying outside the workplace anymore. Seventy-one percent believe workplace mental health support could meaningfully reduce politically driven anxiety. People aren’t leaving that stress at the door; they are bringing it into the office with them.

4. Managers are struggling. Eighty-two percent of managers say the job is increasingly difficult, and just 37 percent feel prepared to recognize their team members’ burnout. The rise in psychological utilization occurs when personal stressors are carried into the workplace. The case for socializing internally Only a small percentage of employees use their EAP benefit. While stigma is real, it’s also an awareness problem.

According to Spring Health’s 2026 Workplace Mental Health Annual Report, 61% of HR leaders report rising mental health leaves, and 59% of employees cite growing financial stress, with the majority of them indicating it’s affecting their mental health. Many of us are racing to deliver more in the same amount of time: to prove our value, retain our jobs, and help the company survive in these turbulent times. Managers who notice someone struggling can make a warm, non-punitive referral. Say plainly what the EAP covers beyond counseling. Naming the full scope, in plain language, is often the only marketing this benefit needs. None of this requires a bigger budget.
