Introduction Despite an increasing emphasis on evidence-based interventions in mental health care, fewer than half of adults starting psychotherapy achieve reliable improvement in their first course of care1. While some treatments may work better than others, genuine differences in efficacy exist for only a handful of disorders2, suggesting that a combination of individual patient characteristics3,4,5 and therapists’ performance6,7 moderates how well a given treatment protocol works. Overall, the quality of the relationship between patient and provider remains a consistent predictor of clinical outcomes8,9,10. This suggests, however, that the strongest predictors of a patient’s clinical outcomes depend on which clinician they happen to meet. A strong therapeutic alliance, defined by mutual agreement on goals, the tasks to achieve those goals, and a positive bond11,12, frequently determines whether a patient stays in treatment13 and whether meaningful improvement occurs8,9,10. This relationship extends beyond the provider’s theoretical orientation or training in specific evidence-based protocols. However, the alliance can only be measured after treatment has begun, making it a lagging metric. When it becomes evident that a patient-provider match is poor, patients drop out of treatment early13 after investing time, money, and emotional energy, thus losing the chance to improve. Indeed, the average dropout rate for psychotherapy for depression is around 17–20 percent14, and higher for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)15. Most mental health systems still assign patients to the first available slot; however, they leave the therapeutic alliance to chance and economics, despite previous meta-analyses16 and empirical studies17,18 suggesting that providers’ historical performance meaningfully predicts future outcomes. Few implementations have assessed this approach at scale5 for various reasons, such as a lack of a centralized electronic health record (EHR) and consistent measurement-based care (MBC) to create these needed datasets. We report the first implementation of a patient-provider matching algorithm at scale. The algorithm recommends providers based on their proven success with clinically similar patients. Embedded within a centralized, employer-sponsored mental health benefit, the algorithm generated a patient-provider “fit” score after an initial clinical assessment, ranking over 6000 licensed therapists and surfacing the top four providers specific to each patient. For patients initiating care between January 2021 and November 2024, over 24,000 chose a therapist from the recommended matches or self-selected based on their own browsing. We compared symptom improvement, likelihood of reliable change or recovery, and cost savings for patients who used matched providers compared to self-selected providers. To determine the specificity of the effects, outcomes were evaluated for patients who screened positive for depression, anxiety, or PTSD. Methods Study design This retrospective cohort study was approved by the Yale Institutional Review Board (IRB protocol ID: 2000029276) and classified as not involving research with human subjects. Informed consent was not required, as the data were anonymized prior to analysis. The research adhered to the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines for observational studies. Program design Data came from an employer-sponsored digital mental health benefit (Spring Health; Spring Care Inc) that includes free or low-cost access to psychotherapy and medication management through video or in-person sessions, care navigation, and digital self-help mental wellness resources. Care is coordinated through a centralized data system in which all provider notes, patient data, assessment results, and patient scheduling are integrated. This centralized system supports several evidence-based components to increase access to and utilization of mental healthcare: provider availability in about one day nationwide, direct patient booking into their selected provider’s appointment, and implementation of measurement-based care. Participants completed an initial assessment (see Questionnaires) and received a personalized care plan according to their responses. They could browse available providers and then select and schedule appointments on their own (see Provider Recommendations). Therapists held master’s or doctoral-level licenses, and all medication providers were either physicians or psychiatric nurse practitioners. To lower the financial barriers to accessing care, participants could book an unlimited number of free appointments with a care navigator and had access to a varying number of employer-sponsored sessions with a therapist and/or medication provider (median = 8, IQR = [7–10]). Additional sessions were covered as an in-network benefit via the health plan and were subject to deductibles, co-pays and co-insurance rules of each health plan. Setting Treatment was primarily delivered through video conferencing, and assessments were collected using the program platform. The study period was from January 1, 2021 and November 1, 2024, and only the first epoch of care (no more than 6 months could elapse between therapy sessions) was considered. Appointment and assessment data were collected up to 6 months after the first therapy appointment. The final study size was determined by how many participants met the inclusion criteria (see Participants). Participants Participants were employees and dependents eligible for the benefit during the study period. Participants were included in the current study if they took an assessment and started treatment within this study period, if they were located in the U.S., were over 18, had a baseline assessment within 30 days prior to starting treatment, if they screened positive for depression and/or anxiety (PHQ-9 ≥ 10 or GAD-7 ≥ 10) and if they had an additional assessment after treatment began. Participants must have started therapy during the study date and remained eligible for the benefit for at least six months after starting, across which period data were collected. Only the first epoch of care (no more than 6 months could elapse between therapy sessions) was considered, and assessments taken up to 6 months after the first therapy appointment were included. Participants did not receive a monetary reward. Questionnaires The program included a digital mental health assessment tool for initial screening and outcome monitoring. For their initial screening, individuals completed a series of self-report questionnaires to identify common mental health difficulties (such as stress, anxiety, eating, or substance use issues), including the Patient Health Questionnaire 9-item scale (PHQ-9)19,20 for depression and the Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7-item scale (GAD-7)21 and targeted questionnaires for any specific issues. (e.g., patients indicating any issues related to trauma were given the PC-PTSD questionnaire). All assessments were optional. For longitudinal outcome monitoring, participants were reminded every 2–4 weeks to complete follow-up questionnaires, consisting of PHQ-9 and/or GAD-7 assessments for most conditions. While some providers encouraged patients to take follow-up assessments, assessments were not required during or at the end of treatment. As a result, many participants stayed in treatment but had sparse assessment data. Measures Depression symptoms were measured with the PHQ-9 (range, 0–27), consisting of nine items assessing the frequency of a range of depression symptoms. Anxiety symptoms were measured with the GAD-7 (range, 0–21), consisting of seven items assessing the frequency of a range of anxiety symptoms. PHQ-9 and GAD-7 scores were outcome variables for assessing symptom change (continuous outcomes), reliable improvement22 (5-point decrease in the PHQ-920 and 4-point decrease in the GAD-7), recovery (achieving a score in the subclinical range19, corresponding to a PHQ-9 score <10 or a GAD7 score of <10), and recovery with reliable improvement. Treatment response (50% reduction in symptomatology) was also included as an outcome variable to facilitate comparison to recent meta-analyses23 (Supplemental Results). Depression and anxiety symptoms were modeled separately. For patients scoring positive for PTSD, GAD-7 was used as a pragmatic proxy to capture symptoms because the GAD-7 assessment was taken more consistently across treatment and yielded substantially more longitudinal coverage than PTSD-specific measures. In contrast, condition-specific instruments for PTSD (e.g., PCL-5) were completed by a smaller subset of patients, limiting statistical power and comparability across providers. The primary outcome was change in clinical symptoms over time (log-days in treatment, measured from the start of therapy [t = 0]). Log-day refers to a nonlinear, log-transformed version of treatment time that reflects the fact that clinical change is often faster early in treatment and slows over time. In the clinical outcome models that use log-day, equal changes in log-day correspond to proportionally faster changes early on and slower changes later, allowing the models to better capture early symptom improvement followed by stabilization. Clinical outcomes were estimated at 1-week post-treatment, corresponding to the average duration of care across all patients plus one week [t = 97 days (average duration) + 7 days]. Number of appointments was also used to predict reliable improvement as an alternative measure of time in care. Therapeutic alliance (range, 0–10) was the average score across three items on which patients rated their providers on (mutual goals, good working relationship, and agreement on best approach). Note that not all patients provided feedback on their alliance with their providers, so in analyses including therapeutic alliance as a factor, only those patient-provider dyads with scores were included. Provider recommendations Participants selected therapists through an online appointment booking system that allows participants to search for a provider based on filters such as availability, location, and provider characteristics (gender, race/ethnicity, conditions treated, etc.). Providers were listed based on the next available appointment. In addition, 4 providers, representing the best potential clinical match to that specific participant, were recommended to participants via a “Your Top Match” flag as part of the therapist profile. Thus, participants could choose to start care with either a “self-selected” therapist (from the overall list of providers) or a “matched” therapist (from the recommendations). The recommendation system had some limitations due primarily to patient browsing patterns, resulting in many patient-provider pairs lacking a selection method designation (Fig. 1, final step). Patients searched freely for therapists without booking an appointment and commonly searched at different times before committing to start care. This freedom, combined with the dynamic nature of the recommendation algorithm, made assigning a selection method to patient-provider pairs difficult. For example, (1) providers could show up as recommended at one point, then shift to the self-selection list at another point (or vice versa) as their historical data and fit scores were updated, (2) providers may not have had any availability when the patient first searched for a provider, but became available later, or (3) a new provider could have shown up in the self-selected list, then shifted to the recommendations after the algorithm features were updated to better promote new providers. Additionally, if the recommendation feature was not yet available for a specific employer, it was not possible to classify the provider as matched or self-selected. As a result, the providers who ultimately delivered care may have been biased toward those who consistently appeared as available and those who demonstrated more consistent historical performance (either stronger or weaker) in order to rise to the recommendation level or always remain outside of it. Fig. 1 Full size image Diagram depicting patient participant flow through the study from identification to study inclusion. Patient-provider matching The recommended providers were based on a score calculated using a weighted combination of the (1) provider’s rate of continuity of care, (2) the provider’s historical patient performance, and (3) the clinical alignment between patient and provider. Continuity of care was defined as how often a provider’s patients continue treatment for at least three appointments within 90 days. This measure was not personalized per se to the patient searching for a provider, but calculated over all of the provider’s prior patients. Historical performance was defined as the percentile rank of provider-level historical improvement in depression symptoms or the percentile rank of provider-level historical improvement in anxiety symptoms. If the patient scored positive for depression, the historical performance for depression improvement was used, and the same for anxiety (although not for any more specific subsets of conditions). Clinical alignment was the similarity between the provider’s self-report of their areas of specialty and the mental health conditions that flagged positive during that specific patient’s intake assessment. For both provider and patient, there were four categories: depression or anxiety, substance use disorders, eating disorders, and/or post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). To calculate the clinical alignment between a patient and provider, the conditions were coded as vectors of 1’s or 0’s, yielding a vector of four values for both provider and patient, and the cosine similarity was calculated between the two vectors. For instance, a therapist specializing in substance use disorder and anxiety would score higher for a patient flagged for these two conditions compared to a therapist specializing in just one or the other. Fit scores were calculated using continuity of care, historical improvement percentile, and clinical alignment. This provided a fit score between 0 and 1, where 0 represents the worst possible fit, and 1 represents the best possible fit. For providers with little to no historical data, an additional slot was added to recommendations to support newer providers, ensure balanced utilization, and help prevent over-recommending of top therapists. Scores were dynamically calculated by the platform backend for many patient-provider pairs (but not all, see Fig. 1, final step), and those with the top scores were surfaced as recommendations to patients. Patients were not aware of the underlying numeric score. Missing data Although this study was missing demographic data and many people were excluded from analyses due to a lack of an appropriately timed baseline assessment, the type of missing data most likely to bias the results was missing data due to assessment drop-out, where patients did not complete any follow-up assessment after starting care. 55% of potential patients were excluded for this reason (Fig. 1). Assessment drop-out could correspond to treatment drop-out, and if the matched and self-selected groups actually differed in terms of the amount of treatment they received, but this was obscured by the follow-up assessment requirement, it could bias our results. The impact of this missingness was assessed by reweighting the data according to the treatment dosage distribution of those without follow-up assessments (Supplemental Results). Statistical analyses Predictor variables were mean-centered and standardized prior to analysis. Provider selection method [matched vs. self-selected] was binarized and mean-centered. We used 3-level mixed-effects regression models to estimate clinical outcomes, with random intercepts to account for clustering of repeated observations (level-1) within participants (level-2) and providers (level-3). An identity link was used for continuous outcomes (depression and anxiety symptoms) and a logit link for categorical outcomes (reliable change). Symptom change, modeled using log-days since the start of treatment, was the main effect of interest. To determine whether choosing a matched therapist was associated with symptom change, the provider selection method by log-days was included as an interaction term. Reliable improvement and recovery were predicted separately using logistic models with log-days since the start of treatment as the main effect. Regression coefficients from these models were converted to probabilities to estimate the percentage of participants who showed reliable improvement from depression and anxiety symptoms. Reliable improvement was also predicted using the number of appointments, with marginal effects estimated using the delta method24. The treatment effect size was quantified using Cohen’s d, calculated by dividing the total treatment improvement in the measure of interest by the baseline SD25. Effect sizes were categorized using established thresholds of small (d < 0.50), medium (0.50 < d < 0.8), and large (d > 0.8). All statistical tests were 2-sided with statistical significance set at α levels of .05. All analyses were conducted in R, version 2024.04.226. Results Participant and provider characteristics Of 13,002,939 total eligible people, 1,305,481 (10%) enrolled in the benefit during the study period. Among those, 24,303 met the eligibility criteria (Fig. 1) and had an appointment with a provider who could be classified as chosen from recommendations or self-selected. Participants were treated by 6119 providers. Providers were predominantly female (82.3%). 51.3% were white, 22.9% were black, 8.2% were Hispanic or Latino, and 5.2% were Asian. The top credentials were LICSW (36.4%), LMHC (37.8%) and LMFT (9.6%). On average, they had 9.3 months of tenure at Spring Health and had received their licensure 9.7 years prior. Across the provider network, approximately 58% of therapists were shown in recommendations; 20% of providers included in recommendations were new to the network. Participants’ age ranged from 18–80 years (mean = 37.2, SD = 11.4). 1943 of 2702 (71.9%) participants with known gender information were female; and 3066 of 5159 (59.4%) participants with known race information were white. 19,334 participants screened positive for depression (scores ≥ 10 points) and 18,538 screened positive for anxiety (scores ≥ 10 points). 13,569 screened positive for both depression and anxiety, corresponding to a 55.8% comorbidity rate, similar to the general population27,28,29. Among the participants screening positive, baseline scores were moderate to severe for both PHQ-9 (mean [SD], 15.4 [4.3]) and GAD-7 (mean [SD], 14.6 [3.3]). Overall utilization During the study period, the average number of business days to the next available appointment was 1.2 days (SD = 0.4 days). The average number of therapy sessions was 6.7 (SD = 4.7), and the average number of medication management sessions (among those who had any) was 2.7 (SD = 2.0). Participants spent approximately 3 months in treatment (97 [58] days), with 1-week post-treatment defined as 104 days. Including the baseline assessment, the average number of total assessments was 3.3. Algorithmically matched vs. self-selected therapists The median fit score was 0.81 (IQR: 0.72-0.86) for self-selected therapists and 0.85 (IQR: 0.82–0.90) for matched therapists. 13,305 patients used self-selected therapists (16,225 patient-participant dyads), 12,662 used matched therapists (12,885 dyads), and 1664 patients had appointments with both kinds (Supplemental Table 1). The difference in the number of dyads reflects the fact that some participants had appointments with multiple providers: patients using matched therapists had appointments with an average of 1.02 providers, whereas patients using self-selected therapists had appointments with an average of 1.14 providers. Patients who started care with matched therapists spent 96.6 days in care, and those who started care with self-selected therapists spent 97.2 days; those with matched therapists attended an average of 6.6 sessions, while those with self-selected therapists attended 7.1 sessions. 21.4% of those with self-selected therapists and 18.7% of those with recommended therapists also accessed a psychiatry/medication session (χ2 = 30.56, p < 0.001). Those with matched therapists took on average 3.4 assessments (including baseline), and those with self-selected therapists took 3.3. For participants scoring positive for depression, depression symptoms decreased by -1.48 points (95% −1.49 to −1.46, p < 0.001; Table 2) with each log-day in care. Symptom reduction was 8.5% faster in matched versus self-selected therapists (b = −0.12, 95% CI: −0.15 to −0.09, p < 0.001) and resulted in a 0.68-point difference (d = 0.2) in depression symptoms by the end of treatment. For reliable change, there was a significant interaction between provider selection method (matched and self-selected) by log-day (OR = 1.09, 95% CI: 1.05–1.14, p < 0.001; Table 2), corresponding to 86.9% of patients using matched therapists achieving reliable change by 1-week post-treatment, compared to 82.6% of patients using a self-selected therapist (absolute difference = 4.3%) (Fig. 2A). To facilitate more direct comparison of these values to recent meta-analyses23, we also modeled the results using treatment response at two months (Supplemental Results: Treatment response). Fig. 2: Probability of reliable change for patients choosing a matched therapist vs. a self-selected therapist. Full size image For patients with A depression, B anxiety, and C PTSD, probability of reliable change is plotted as a function of time (days) in treatment for matched therapists (cyan) vs. self-selected therapists (red). Vertical line represents 1-week posttreatment (average: 103 days). The probability of reliable change increased as a function of time, with a significant time by provider selection method [matched vs. self-selected] interaction, indicating that choosing a matched provider increased the probability of reliable change for all three conditions. For recovery, there was also a significant interaction between provider selection method (matched and self-selected) by log-day (OR = 1.13, 95% CI: 1.08–1.17, p < 0.001), corresponding to 84.6% of patients using matched therapists achieving recovery compared to 78.2% with self-selected therapists (absolute difference = 6.4%). When considering reliable change and recovery together, 74.1% of patients using matched therapists achieved reliable change and recovery by 1-week post-treatment, compared to 66.6% of patients using a self-selected therapist (absolute difference = 7.5%). For participants scoring positive for anxiety, symptoms decreased by -1.31 points (95% CI: −1.31 to −1.27, p < 0.001) (Table 1) with each log-day in care. Symptom reduction was 7.5% faster in matched versus self-selected therapists (b = −0.10, 95% CI: −0.13 to −0.06, p < 0.001), and resulted in a difference of 0.49 points at post-treatment (d = 0.15). In terms of reliable change, there was a significant interaction between provider selection method (matched and self-selected) by log-day (OR = 1.09, 95% CI: 1.05–1.14, p < 0.001; Table 2), corresponding to 87.9% of patients using matched therapists achieving reliable change by 1-week post-treatment, compared to 84.0% of patients using a self-selected therapist (difference = 3.9%) (Fig. 2B). For recovery, there was also a significant interaction between provider selection method (matched and self-selected) by log-day (OR = 1.10, 95% CI: 1.06–1.15, p = 0.001), corresponding to 82.2% of patients using matched therapists achieving recovery compared to 77.0% with self-selected therapists (absolute difference = 5.2%). When considering reliable change and recovery together, 76.3% of patients using matched therapists achieved reliable change and recovery by 1-week post-treatment, compared to 70.4% of patients using a self-selected therapist (absolute difference = 5.9%). Table 1 Symptom change as a function of time and provider selection method Full size table Table 2 Reliable change by time in treatment and provider selection method Full size table For participants with PTSD, anxiety symptoms decreased by −1.31 points (95% −1.33 to −1.28, p < 0.001) (Table 1) with each log-day in care. Symptom reduction was 6.4% faster with matched vs. self-selected therapists (b = −0.08, 95% CI: −0.13 to −0.03, p < 0.001), corresponding to a difference of 0.50 points at post-treatment (d = 0.15). In terms of reliable change, there was a significant interaction between provider selection method (matched and self-selected) by log-day (OR = 1.09, 95% CI: 1.04–1.15, p = 0.001; Table 2), corresponding to 87.3% of patients using matched therapists achieving reliable change by 1-week post-treatment, compared to 82.8% of patients using a self-selected therapist (difference = 4.5%) (Fig. 2C). For recovery, there was also as a significant interaction between provider selection method (matched and self-selected) by log-day (OR = 1.09, 95% CI: 1.04–1.16, p = 0.001), corresponding to 77.3% of patients using matched therapists achieving recovery compared to 71.3% with self-selected therapists (absolute difference = 6.0%). When considering reliable change and recovery together, 72.1% of patients using matched therapists achieved reliable change and recovery by 1-week post-treatment, compared to 65.3% of patients using a self-selected therapist (absolute difference = 6.8%). Components of patient-provider fit Overall, choosing a matched therapist led to greater symptom reduction and a higher likelihood of achieving reliable change and recovery. Furthermore, within the group using matched therapists, the better the fit between the patient and provider (i.e., a score generated from continuity of care, historical improvement, and clinical alignment), the better the therapeutic alliance (b = 0.05, 95% CI: 0.04–0.06, p < 0.001). This indicates that higher fit scores served as a leading indicator of a stronger patient-provider relationship. Which of these components of the patient-provider fit contributed to clinical improvement? Within the matched group, regression analysis revealed continuity of care and provider historical performance significantly predicted reliable change (continuity: OR = 1.037, 95% CI: 1.013–1.062, p = 0.003; historical performance: OR = 1.039, 95% CI: 1.014–1.065, p = 0.002), and alignment did not (p = 0.684). Across both matched and self-selected groups, the pattern of results was similar (Supplemental Table 2, continuity: OR = 1.043, 95% CI: 1.018–1.069, p = 0.001; historical performance: OR = 1.051, 95% CI: 1.027–1.075, p < 0.001; alignment OR = 1.003, 95% CI: 0.985–1.023, p = 0.727). When these components were included in the model, the selection method remained significant (OR = 1.074, 95% CI: 1.017–1.134, p = 0.010), suggesting that the clinical benefit of matched vs. self-selected therapists is not fully explained by the components used to generate the match. However, the selection method did not interact with any of the components (ps > 0.254), indicating that the benefit of higher continuity of care and historical performance does not depend on the selection method. Cost savings for matching providers Provider matching also reduced the total cost of the care per patient who reliably improved, with 12.9% lower cost per reliable change and 10.8% lower cost per recovery for those using matched providers compared to those using self-selected providers (Supplementary Table 3; Supplementary Results). Discussion We evaluated the first implementation of a patient-provider matching algorithm at scale. Patients who chose an algorithm-recommended therapist improved faster, were more likely to achieve reliable change or recovery, and cost less to treat than those who self-selected a provider, despite receiving the same benefit design. While the size of these effects was small, they were consistent and statistically significant across depression, anxiety, and PTSD, providing evidence of modest, incremental advantages of algorithm-recommended matching rather than large, transformative changes at the individual level. By leveraging data on historical provider performance, such as the provider’s rate of continuity of care, their historical patient-improvement percentile, and the clinical alignment between patient and provider, the algorithm recommends providers who are better able to keep patients from dropping out of care early (a persistent problem for psychotherapy14) and who consistently achieve successful results with patients of similar profiles. Moreover, because the algorithm relied on dynamic, pragmatic input and promoted new providers, the majority of therapists (58%) appeared in recommendations at one point or another. Rather than overloading a small subset of exceptional providers, matching as implemented in this study allows a wide variety of therapists to better build a strong patient-provider relationship, as evidenced by the positive relationship between fit score and therapeutic alliance—even though “fit” was calculated prior to the initiation of treatment. By improving the accuracy of patient–provider matching at treatment initiation, the algorithm increases system efficiency and reduces early mismatches and allows most therapists to have more impact. The key components driving the success of the patient-provider match were the provider’s rate of continuity of care and their historical patient-improvement, but not the clinical alignment between patient and provider, which was calculated based on the patient’s initial assessment and the specialties that providers self-endorse. This result suggests that although matching patients with providers with appropriate specialization may create the potential for better outcomes, the actual driver of improvement is the provider’s record of successfully treating similar patients (using historical performance specific to the patients’ condition) and their ability to keep such patients engaged in care (possibly a more general skill of the provider). An alternative, statistical interpretation is that by using historical performance specifically for depressive patients or anxious patients, alignment is already implicitly included in the model, and so when it is added as a standalone variable, it is unable to explain further variance. When considered together in the form of a “fit score,” these components predicted therapeutic alliance. In other words, the matching algorithm helps lay the groundwork for a positive alliance, and consistent engagement allows that alliance to flourish and translate into clinical gains. The effect size for the advantage of using matched rather than self-selected therapists is comparable to or exceeds those seen among different therapy modalities (e.g., from near-zero30 to d = 0.202) in meta-analyses. This finding shows that how patients and providers are paired can matter to a similar degree as differences observed between specific evidence-based treatments—especially in large, heterogeneous samples—while also underscoring that such effects are typically modest on average. Studies examining whether patient characteristics can be used to match individuals to one evidence-based treatment over another have similarly found small average effects, despite statistical significance, alongside substantial heterogeneity in who benefits most from matching31. Thus, matching strategies—whether focused on treatment modality or provider characteristics—are unlikely to produce large mean differences across all patients, but may nonetheless yield meaningful benefits when applied within specific subgroups or at scale. In our study, a centralized care model in which all providers used a shared electronic health record (EHR) and measurement-based care (MBC) was routine, improved care delivery within the benefit program and enabled patient-provider matching. Recent meta-analyses23 show that treatment response rate in psychotherapies at 2 (±1) months after baseline was 41% (95% CI: 38 ~ 43). In comparison, we saw high rates of reliable change and recovery: across all clinical conditions, over 65% of patients achieved reliable change with recovery, with approximately 6.5% more patients achieving the same outcomes with matched therapists. After better equating for methodology differences (Supplementary Results), patients with self-selected therapists exhibited a similar treatment response rate (46.3%), while those using matched therapists continued to see an advantage (54.9%). Beyond methodological differences, outcomes may also reflect differences in the study population and care delivery model: participants accessed employer-sponsored care with no out-of-pocket costs, rapid treatment initiation, and sustained, measurement-based support, likely reducing common barriers such as delays, financial strain, and early dropout. Integrating features that enhance access and support engagement alongside psychotherapy yields outcomes that meet or exceed clinical benchmarks32. This centralized care model also conferred both the means to refine matching algorithms continuously and the operational flexibility to guide patients toward the providers most likely to help them. Because providers are largely contractors, the program can routinely triage care toward the best-fitting providers without needing to worry about filling caseloads of poorer-performing providers or those who are simply a good fit for fewer patients. The program can quantify and capitalize on a diversity of therapeutic approaches and provider qualities by directly measuring key outcomes, rather than controlling a specific care protocol. Moreover, employing an algorithm to match patients to providers on straightforward metrics may yield incremental improvements in outcomes without requiring additional provider training or added effort from patients. Finally, the scale of the benefit program enables even modest effects to be translated into substantial population-level gains, given the high volume of patients who engage in care33. For example, a 4.3% absolute difference in reliable improvement for those patients who used matched therapists compared to self-selected therapists corresponds to tens of thousands of people when considered across the population eligible for the benefit. Taken together, these findings suggest both constraints and opportunities for implementing algorithm-guided provider matching in standard clinical settings. Limited caseload capacity and therapist availability may constrain the ability to act on matching recommendations, and the use of relative provider rankings may be more sensitive in in-person settings where clinicians are more likely to know one another. In addition, successful adoption depends on consistent use of MBC and supporting data infrastructure, and as we have shown, expected effect sizes are small. At the same time, the matching approach in this study uses relatively simple and widely available signals: basic appointment data to capture continuity of care, standardized symptom assessments to measure patient improvement and generate provider historical performance, and straightforward alignment between patient intake needs and provider-reported specialties. As a result, while direct replication may be difficult, core elements of the matching framework could plausibly be adapted to smaller practices to reduce early dropout and strategically optimize caseloads for more impact. A key strength of this evaluation is that it employs real-world data from a large, employer-sponsored mental health program, providing the statistical power to examine multiple conditions and produce generalizable insights. The MBC framework used across all providers ensures consistent data collection and the opportunity for ongoing quality improvement. However, the observational design means the study cannot fully exclude selection bias, whereby patients who opt for recommended providers may differ systematically from those who do not. Moreover, although the algorithm benefits from substantial EHR data, the inclusion criteria for the study result in the exclusion of a substantial number of potential participants, and the applicability of the results may be limited to systems with similar infrastructure and patient demographics. Finally, while fit scores serve as a useful leading indicator of the therapeutic alliance, certain unmeasured factors (e.g., unique interpersonal skills of the provider, patient motivation, external life stressors) may influence outcomes and warrant consideration when interpreting the results. Investigating how recommendations perform in specific subpopulations, or how best to incorporate patient preferences and clinical judgment, could offer deeper insights into maximizing the effectiveness of patient-provider matching. In summary, the present results illustrate that a recommendation engine—leveraging a matching algorithm based on prior provider performance with similar patients as tracked through a centralized electronic health record—can shorten the path to symptom improvement. Although the individual-level effects are small, these effects can translate into substantial population-level gains, given the high volume of patients who engage in care33 and can reduce the total cost of care per patient who reliably improved or recovered by more than 12%. Thus, matching patients to providers may reduce overall healthcare costs and patient distress, underscoring the financial and clinical value of implementing a matching algorithm in behavioral healthcare at scale.

data.title: 6 ways to prevent employee burnout
data.ai_summary: Spring Health compiled six strategies to prevent employee burnout, citing research that 61% of HR professionals said burnout increased in the past year. The article notes 30% of employees experience silent burnout and that lack of mental health access raises burnout risk by 69%.
data.author: Hayden Goethe For Spring Health Stacker
data.full_text:
Business 6 ways to prevent employee burnout 6 ways to prevent employee burnout Employee burnout affects entire organizations, with consequences for performance, workplace culture, and the bottom line. At many organizations, employees are emotionally drained, managers are stretched to their limits, and HR teams are overwhelmed by the growing volume of mental health concerns. The old ways of addressing burnout, such as by offering a wellness stipend, a few mental health days, or a traditional EAP, aren't cutting it anymore. Workplace burnout is a business risk that contributes to absenteeism, lost productivity, increased healthcare costs, and high turnover. And for organizations that aren't paying attention, it could quietly drive major disruptions. But burnout is also preventable if you know what to look for and are willing to treat it as the systemic issue it truly is. With that in mind, Spring Health compiled a list of ways to help curb employee burnout for a healthy workplace. What is employee burnout? Employee burnout is a state of chronic stress that results in emotional exhaustion, detachment from work, and reduced performance. It often builds over time, which makes it difficult to identify early. Burnout can also show up in ways that look like disengagement or low motivation. You may notice employees becoming unusually irritable or withdrawn. They might seem less confident in their work, struggle to concentrate, or begin questioning the value of their role. Some may stop speaking up in meetings, miss deadlines, or start calling in sick more often. How prevalent is employee burnout? Research conducted by Spring Health in early 2026 revealed some interesting findings. Among over 500 HR professionals across five countries: 61% said employee burnout had increased in the past year.

48% said employee burnout was the top challenge their employees faced (#1 answer).

They estimated that 30% of all employees are experiencing silent burnout, which is defined as a "slow, undetected state of exhaustion while maintaining the appearance that everything is fine." Burnout often hits the most committed and hardest-working employees first. The high cost of employee burnout When burnout goes unaddressed, it can reduce organizational performance and increase operational costs. HR professionals are feeling the effects too. In one 2023-24 Society for Human Resource Management report, over 50% of HR teams reported working beyond their capacity, with many citing understaffing as a major factor contributing to their own burnout. How to prevent employee burnout Burnout is a reflection of organizational systems. Preventing burnout requires thoughtful, proactive strategies that go beyond perks and check-the-box programs. Here's what that looks like in practice. Provide mental health support that meets the moment Within Spring Health's research, one of the biggest drivers of employee burnout was whether or not the employees had access to an enhanced mental health solution. Spring Health asked over 1,500 employees across five countries what their biggest mental health challenges in the past year were. Employees who said they lacked access to adequate mental health benefits from their employer were 69% more likely to say they had experienced employee burnout in the past year than those employees who did have access to adequate care. This data shows that preventing burnout starts with giving employees access to effective, easy-to-use mental health care. Traditional employee assistance programs often fall short, with limited provider networks, long wait times, and confusing processes that discourage use, especially when someone is already overwhelmed. Prioritize manager support and training Managers are your first line of defense against burnout, but they're also some of the most impacted. They're balancing their own workloads while trying to support employees, navigate change, and maintain team morale. Equipping managers with the right tools and specialized mental health training to recognize burnout signs, create safe team dynamics, and have supportive mental health conversations can make a huge difference. When managers feel supported themselves, they're far better positioned to support others. Reassess workloads and expectations In many organizations, high performers are rewarded with more responsibilities but not necessarily more time or resources. This imbalance risks burning out your best people and reinforces a culture where overwork is normalized. Instead, take time to evaluate role expectations, adjust workloads, and ensure priorities are realistic. Encourage teams to focus on outcomes instead of output. And make sure high performers aren't silently paying the price for their success. Go beyond surface-level mental health support Traditional EAPs often involve long wait times, confusing access processes, and limited session availability. For someone already burned out, these barriers can feel insurmountable. A more effective approach includes fast access to high-quality care, personalized support plans, and seamless coordination between HR, managers, and providers. Employees shouldn't have to work harder just to feel better. Create space to rest and recharge Creating a culture where people actually feel safe taking PTO is an important method for preventing burnout. This might mean modeling time off at the leadership level, encouraging boundaries between work and personal life, and giving people the flexibility to manage their energy in ways that work for them. For some, that might be a mental health day. For others, it might be shifting hours or working from home when needed. The point is that time to rest should feel like part of how work gets done. Build a culture of fairness and connection Burnout often stems from feeling undervalued, invisible, or stuck. It's intensified by favoritism, lack of transparency, or inequities in pay and promotion. Creating a culture that actively supports human connection, along with fairness and inclusion, is essential. This means listening to employee feedback, addressing systemic gaps, and giving people meaningful ways to grow. Burnout prevention is a business strategy Organizations that invest in preventing employee burnout are also making a smart business decision. Burnout directly impacts your most critical organizational and HR metrics: retention, productivity, engagement, and healthcare costs. When employees are mentally depleted, they're more likely to miss work, disengage, or leave altogether. Replacing them is disruptive and expensive. That's why forward-thinking companies treat mental health as a pillar of operational success. They're embedding it into their leadership practices and culture because they know that preventing burnout strengthens every part of the business. When employees feel supported, they show up with more energy and focus. Teams communicate better, turnover slows, and leaders can focus on growth instead of damage control. Burnout prevention is a people strategy and a performance strategy. And in today's climate, it's one of the most important investments your organization can make. Digital Mental Health Market to Reach USD 58.42 Billion by 2036 Digital Mental Health Market Overview



The global digital mental health market is witnessing strong growth as healthcare systems increasingly adopt technology-driven solutions to address rising mental health challenges worldwide. Valued at USD 13.62 billion in 2025, the market is projected to reach USD 58.42 billion by 2036, growing from USD 16.34 billion in 2026 at a CAGR of 13.6% during the forecast period. The market expansion is primarily driven by the growing prevalence of depression, anxiety, stress-related disorders, and the widening gap between demand for mental healthcare services and the availability of trained professionals.



Mental health has become one of the largest global healthcare concerns. According to global health organizations, more than one billion people worldwide are currently living with mental health conditions, while a significant portion of affected individuals still lack access to professional treatment. Traditional mental healthcare systems continue to face shortages of therapists, psychiatrists, and mental health infrastructure, especially in developing economies. As a result, digital mental health platforms are emerging as scalable and cost-effective alternatives capable of delivering support remotely through smartphones, telehealth systems, mobile applications, and AI-enabled tools.



Digital mental health solutions include tele-therapy platforms, meditation and wellness applications, AI-powered mental health chatbots, digital therapeutics, and wearable-integrated mental wellness monitoring systems. These platforms help users access therapy, cognitive behavioral therapy exercises, mood tracking, guided meditation, and mental wellness support without requiring in-person consultations. The affordability and convenience of digital platforms are significantly improving access to care for underserved populations.



Download Sample Report Here : https://www.meticulousresearch.com/download-sample-report/cp_id=6660



Rising Adoption of AI and Telehealth Platforms



Artificial intelligence is becoming one of the most influential technologies shaping the digital mental health market. AI-powered chatbots, virtual therapists, and machine learning algorithms are helping companies provide personalized and scalable mental health support. These technologies can analyze behavioral patterns, speech, text, and user engagement to detect emotional distress and recommend appropriate interventions. AI tools also support continuous engagement, making mental healthcare more accessible at any time of the day.



Tele-mental health platforms are also transforming the market by enabling licensed therapists to connect with patients through secure video consultations, voice calls, and messaging services. The convenience of remote therapy has accelerated significantly after the COVID-19 pandemic, when telehealth adoption expanded rapidly across several countries. Subscription-based therapy platforms are now attracting millions of users seeking affordable and flexible mental healthcare services from home.



What is Driving the Demand for Digital Mental Health Solutions?



One of the biggest drivers of the market is the growing treatment gap in mental healthcare services. Many individuals experiencing mental health disorders are unable to access traditional therapy due to high treatment costs, social stigma, or the shortage of mental health professionals. Digital solutions help bridge this gap by offering immediate and lower-cost access to support services through mobile devices and online platforms.



Another important growth factor is the increasing awareness of workplace mental health. Employers are investing heavily in digital mental wellness programs to improve employee productivity, reduce absenteeism, and lower healthcare costs. Corporate wellness platforms now provide therapy access, stress management tools, mindfulness programs, and emotional wellbeing support as part of employee benefit packages. This trend is creating a strong commercial opportunity for enterprise-focused digital mental health providers.



Browse in Depth : https://www.meticulousresearch.com/product/digital-mental-health-market-6660



Expansion of Digital Therapeutics and Consumer Wellness Apps



Digital therapeutics are expected to become one of the fastest-growing segments within the market. Unlike traditional wellness apps, digital therapeutics are clinically validated software-based treatments designed to manage or treat specific mental health conditions such as depression, anxiety, insomnia, and substance abuse disorders. Several products are gaining regulatory approvals and reimbursement support, increasing their adoption in clinical care settings.



At the same time, self-guided mental wellness applications continue to dominate the consumer market due to their convenience and accessibility. Applications focused on meditation, stress reduction, sleep improvement, and mindfulness are attracting millions of global users. These platforms allow individuals to manage their mental wellbeing independently through guided exercises and behavioral therapy techniques delivered digitally.



Depression and anxiety management remain the largest application areas in the market because these disorders affect hundreds of millions of people globally. Increasing stress levels, changing lifestyles, social isolation, and work-related burnout are contributing to the rising demand for digital support solutions targeting these conditions.



Regional Outlook and Competitive Landscape



North America is expected to maintain the largest share of the digital mental health market due to strong telehealth adoption, high mental health awareness, favorable reimbursement frameworks, and rising employer-sponsored mental health programs. The United States continues to lead the regional market as consumers increasingly adopt online therapy and digital wellness services.



Asia-Pacific is projected to witness the fastest growth during the forecast period. Countries such as China, India, Singapore, and Australia are investing in digital healthcare infrastructure and expanding mobile health initiatives. Rapid smartphone penetration, large underserved populations, and growing awareness regarding mental wellness are creating substantial growth opportunities across the region.



The competitive landscape includes telehealth providers, AI-based mental wellness companies, consumer wellness app developers, and digital therapeutic firms. Major companies operating in the market include Teladoc Health, Talkspace, Headspace Health, Calm.com, Woebot Health, Spring Health, and Lyra Health. These companies are focusing on AI integration, strategic partnerships, clinical validation, and subscription-based business models to strengthen their market presence.

Future Outlook of the Digital Mental Health Market



The future of the digital mental health market appears highly promising as governments, healthcare providers, employers, and consumers increasingly recognize the importance of accessible mental healthcare. Technological advancements in AI, digital therapeutics, virtual reality therapy, and wearable-based monitoring systems are expected to further enhance treatment personalization and patient engagement.



As healthcare systems continue shifting toward remote and technology-enabled care models, digital mental health platforms are likely to become an essential component of mainstream healthcare delivery. The market's long-term growth will be supported by rising mental health awareness, increasing smartphone adoption, expanding reimbursement support, and the continued need for scalable mental healthcare solutions worldwide.

data.ai_summary: Spring Health released research conducted in early 2026 with over 500 HR/benefits professionals and 1,500+ full-time employees, finding that 74% of employees report financial stress has impacted their mental health, and 59% say financial stress has increased over the past five years.
data.author: Written Byhayden Goethecontent Marketing Lead

industries.name: Worksite Financial Wellness & Employee Assistance Programs (EAP)

data.full_text:
According to research Spring Health conducted in early 2026 of 500+ HR/benefits professionals and 1,500+ full-time employees, 74% of employees say financial stress has impacted their mental health. This isn't a fringe issue. And it's not just about compensation. Employee financial stress can create productivity and presenteeism for organizations while leading to employee burnout, sleep issues, and more for employees. And it can affect a wide swath of the employee population, no matter how much they’re paid. This is an organizational performance risk worth every organization’s attention. What is employee financial stress? Employee financial stress isn’t just economic. It’s psychological. Employee financial stress is the ongoing cognitive and emotional strain caused by debt, caregiving costs, housing and inflation pressures, income insecurity, and unpredictable expenses. Spring Health's research found that 59% of employees say financial stress has increased over the past five years. From a clinical perspective, stress intensifies when people feel a lack of control. When employees believe their financial situation is uncontrollable, stress shifts from temporary to chronic. That chronic stress alters sleep, increases anxiety, impacts decision-making, and amplifies relational strain. How financial stress shows up at work Financial stress rarely stays at home. It follows employees into meetings, inboxes, and decision cycles. Presenteeism: Employees may be physically present but mentally preoccupied. Ongoing worry about bills, debt, or caregiving costs consumes cognitive bandwidth. Over time, this “always-on” background stress leads to slower decision-making, reduced creativity, diminished focus, and sustained performance drag, even if attendance remains steady.

Sleep disruption: Financial worry is a common drivers of sleep issues, which was the top mental health challenge identified by employees in our survey. When someone experiences difficulty falling asleep or staying asleep, mood regulation declines, focus narrows, and stress tolerance drops. The longer poor sleep persists, the more other symptoms escalate.

What begins as worry can quickly become exhaustion.

What begins as worry can quickly become exhaustion. Productivity erosion: Over time, the combined impact of cognitive strain, poor sleep, and emotional depletion shows up in missed deadlines, reduced engagement or increased isolation, and higher risk of leaves of absence. Financial stress becomes not just a personal burden, but a workforce stability issue. Watch below: Hebba Youssef, who is Chief People Officer at Workweek and founder/creator of "I Hate It Here," reacts to recent Spring Health findings that showed that 59% of employees say financial stress has increased over the past five years. Also, 74% of employees say that financial stress has significantly or somewhat impacted their mental health. Watch the full webinar here. Populations that are vulnerable to financial stress Interestingly, household income seems to play very little role when examining the impact of financial stress. Coincidentally, within our research among U.S. employees, the same percentage responded saying they experienced financial stress with household incomes under $50,000 as did those whose household incomes were at least $150,000. However, within our research, the following employee segments were among the highest reporting that financial stress was affecting their mental health: 86% of respondents in the technology industry

79% of respondents in the finance industry

82% of all employees under the age of 45

86% of India respondents

83% of Mexico respondents Why traditional EAP models fall short Traditional EAPs often offer generic financial articles, provide short-term counseling without specialization, lack tailored provider matching, and require employees to self-navigate complex systems. Here's the clinical reality: If someone struggling with financial stress is matched to a provider who doesn't specialize in economic anxiety, debt-related shame, relationship strain tied to finances, or caregiving financial pressure, they're less likely to engage. Wrong-fit care drives drop-off. What helps? A precision-based approach to financial stress 1. Early identification through quick assessment Mental health stigma is real. “Trying to get employees to talk about financial stress is like trying to stop a tsunami,” one benefits manager said during our recent webinar to announce the release of our annual report. That’s why leading employers offer brief, clinically validated assessments that identify financial stress as a driver of anxiety or depression early. This prevents escalation into employee burnout, leave of absence, and crisis intervention. 2. Personalized provider matching This is critical. Employees facing financial stress need providers who specialize in financial anxiety, stress tied to debt or economic instability, relationship strain connected to money, caregiver-related financial overwhelm, and high-acuity conditions that financial stress may exacerbate. Provider matching matters. If a female employee struggling with financial stress and food insecurity is sent to a provider whose background or specialty is unrelated (such as substance use in a different population), engagement drops. Precision matching increases trust, follow-through, and symptom improvement. Within our research, among employees who said financial stress was impacting their mental health, 58% said they had met with a mental health professional, such as a therapist or counselor, in the past year. 3. Integrated financial guidance and mental healthcare Financial stress is both practical and emotional. Support should include: Budgeting or financial navigation resources

Work-life financial services

Therapy with clinicians trained in financial stress dynamics

Coaching for habit and resilience building

Retirement-planning coaching and resources 4. Reducing friction with a single front door Financial stress already creates cognitive overload. If accessing help requires multiple phone calls, searching portals, and explaining your situation repeatedly, engagement drops. Leading employers provide one clear starting point, route employees to appropriate care quickly, and coordinate paperwork and administrative burden. This restores a sense of control. What leading employers are doing differently They track financial stress as a workforce risk signal. They move beyond generic EAPs. They invest in precision mental healthcare with measurement-based outcomes. They choose AI-native mental health solutions that match employees to providers who are specialized in their needs. They treat financial stress as upstream risk, not downstream crisis. And the proof is in the data. In Spring Health’s survey, employees who said they lacked access to adequate mental health support from their employer were 52% more likely to say they experienced financial stress. Employees can't control inflation, market shifts, debt obligations, or caregiving costs. But employers can control whether: Financial support is easy to access

Provider matching is thoughtful and specialized

Employees feel guided or left to navigate alone Employee financial stress may be unavoidable. But unmanaged financial stress doesn't have to be.

Infusion Services Search Q1 2026 Behavioral Health M&A Report May 7

5 min read

Behavioral Health M&A Executive Summary: A Year of Resilience and Reality Checks

A total of 42 closed transactions — 34 traditional M&A deals and 8 growth deals — were reported in Q1 2026. Traditional M&A volume increased from 29 closed deals in Q4 2025, though it remained below the 40 deals closed in Q1 2025. The 8 growth deals carried a combined disclosed value of approximately $535.7 million, led by major financing rounds for Talkiatry and Grow Therapy, signaling continued institutional conviction in scaled virtual behavioral health platforms.

"Q1 was a solid start to the year — not a blowout, but active. Traditional deal volume bounced back from Q4, and what stands out to me is how concentrated the mental health activity is becoming around platform builders. Beacon Behavioral closed four add-ons in a single quarter, and you're seeing the same pattern across ABA. On the growth side, Talkiatry and Grow Therapy together raised $360 million. That's a signal that institutional capital still has a lot of appetite for virtual and tech-enabled delivery models at scale." — Mertz Taggart Managing Partner Kevin Taggart said. Mental health led all sub-sectors with 19 closed traditional M&A deals, followed by Autism/IDD with 10 and Addiction Treatment with 5. PE-backed strategics and platform builders drove the bulk of transaction volume, consistent with the consolidation patterns seen throughout 2025.

Addiction Treatment M&A

Five addiction treatment deals closed in Q1 2026, down from 7 in Q4 2025 and 8 in Q1 2025. The subdued volume reflects ongoing caution among SUD-focused buyers, many of whom continue to work through platform integrations before resuming add-on activity.



"SUD deal flow has been building momentum, and the buyers we're talking to are increasingly motivated to get back into the space. Some platforms that were focused on integration over the past couple of years are starting to look at add-ons again, and we're seeing new entrants with capital ready to deploy. For a quality addiction treatment provider considering a sale, I think the timing is actually quite good — there's demand out there and it's growing." — Taggart said. The most notable deal of the quarter was Mayfair Group's acquisition of Praesum Healthcare, a Florida-based multi-state addiction treatment platform operating more than 30 centers across the Eastern U.S. under brands including Sunrise Detox, The Counseling Center, and Evolve Recovery Center. Praesum had filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in August 2025 and was acquired out of the bankruptcy auction for $18.5 million.

Additional Q1 addiction treatment transactions:

● Lee Equity Partners-backed Bradford Health Services acquired Parkdale Center, expanding its inpatient SUD footprint. ● Victory Recovery Partners acquired Realization Center, an addiction treatment provider with locations in Manhattan and Brooklyn, continuing its multi-specialty behavioral health rollup in the Northeast. ● Xolani acquired Welwynn Outpatient Center in the outpatient SUD space. ● Doctor Staffers LLC acquired TAKS Care Group.



Mental Health M&A Nineteen mental health deals closed in Q1 2026, down from 24 in Q1 2025 and roughly in line with the 18 closed in Q4 2025. The sub-sector continues to account for the majority of BH transaction volume, driven by active PE-backed platform builders and a growing number of nonprofit strategic combinations.



Latticework Capital-backed Beacon Behavioral Partners was the most active acquirer in the quarter, closing four add-ons: Carolina Psychiatry, SunCoast Psychiatry, Novus Neurology, Psychiatry, & TMS, and one yet to be named acquisition — all in outpatient psychiatry. Mertz Taggart provided exclusive sell-side advisory services in the acquisition of an outpatient mental health platform. The parties have requested confidentiality.

Other notable closed mental health transactions:

● Goldman Sachs Asset Management formed a new platform with LearnWell, a provider of behavioral health services for students in hospital and therapeutic day school settings. ● Cerebral acquired Get Inflow, a digital ADHD-focused platform, continuing its build-out of condition-specific virtual care offerings. ● Quantum Health acquired CirrusMD, adding text-based virtual care to its navigation platform. ● Harbor Health acquired Rippl Care, a dementia-focused behavioral health provider. ● Nocd acquired Rebound Health, expanding its OCD-focused digital platform. ● Victory Recovery Partners acquired North Shore Relationship Center, a group therapy practice in Port Jefferson, New York. ● Chimes International acquired Family Focus, a community-based mental health and social services provider. ● Omni Family of Services acquired Justiceworks Youthcare, a youth-focused mental health provider. ● New View Alliance (formerly Gateway-Longview) acquired New Directions Youth and Family Services, continuing its nonprofit consolidation strategy in children's behavioral health. ● Proficio Therapy Services acquired Child's Play Therapy Services, a pediatric outpatient practice. ● WVU Medicine Wheeling Hospital acquired Orchard Park Hospital, an inpatient psychiatric facility. Also announced — but not yet closed — was Universal Health Services' (UHS) agreement to acquire Talkspace for approximately $835 million. Talkspace operates a nationwide virtual behavioral health platform with roughly 6,000 licensed professionals and generated $229 million in revenue in 2025 and $15 million in EBITDA, which translates to an eye-popping approximately 56x multiple . Expected to close in Q3 2026, the deal reflects the broader thesis that large health systems are moving to integrate virtual outpatient behavioral health capacity with their existing inpatient infrastructure. Also announced was Spring Health's agreement to acquire Alma, a mental health marketplace that would significantly expand Spring Health's provider network. On the growth side, mental health attracted six of the quarter's eight venture rounds. Talkiatry raised a $210 million Series D led by Perceptive Advisors — bringing total funding to over $400 million — to expand its employed-psychiatrist model, which now includes more than 800 full-time W-2 psychiatrists in-network with over 100 insurers. Grow Therapy raised a $150 million Series D led by TCV and Goldman Sachs Alternatives at a reported $3 billion valuation. Salma Health raised $80 million from ARCH Venture Partners. Smaller rounds were completed by Somethings ($19.2M), Jimini Health ($17M), and Coral Care ($13M).



Autism and Intellectual/Developmental Disabilities M&A Ten Autism/I/DD deals closed in Q1 2026, up from 7 in Q4 2025 and below the 12 closed in Q1 2025. New PE platform formations and continued ABA consolidation remained the primary drivers.



"ABA and I/DD continue to attract serious buyer interest — three new PE platforms launched in the space in Q1 alone, which tells you something about where institutional capital is placing its bets. Buyers are doing their diligence carefully, but well-run practices with solid clinical outcomes and clean financials are still generating competitive processes. We're also seeing growing interest in HCBS and community-based I/DD models as buyers look to build out the full continuum." — Taggart said. Three new PE platforms were formed in the space during Q1. Momentum Health Partners launched with the acquisition of Advanced Autism Center for Treatment (AACT). Aquitaine Capital formed a new platform with KidsChoice, an ABA and behavioral therapy provider.

Elysium Management LLC formed a platform with InBloom Autism Services (formerly Behavior Development Group), a multi-state ABA provider.

Centerbridge Partners, Vistria Group, and Madison Dearborn-backed Sevita (formerly The Mentor Network) completed the acquisition of RES-Care Community Living, a significant I/DD and home- and community-based services combination that expands Sevita's national HCBS and supported living footprint.

Additional Q1 Autism/I/DD transactions:

● General Atlantic-backed ACES acquired Ally Pediatric Therapy, continuing its ABA and pediatric therapy expansion. ● Center for Social Dynamics acquired Behavior Change Institute (BCI). ● Renovus Capital Partners-backed Behavioral Framework acquired Autism ETC. ● Step Forward ABA acquired MySpot (NC and VA locations). ● The Verland Foundation acquired Triad Behavior Support Services, a nonprofit I/DD strategic combination. ● NCG Care acquired community-based operations from Broadstep Behavioral Health. On the growth side, Answersnow raised $40 million from HealthQuest Capital to expand its telehealth-based ABA platform, and Avela Health raised $6.5 million from Artemis Fund.

data.full_text:
Over the past five years, digital mental health solutions have surged — not just in number, but in influence. The global mental health app market is expected to surpass $17.5 billion by 2030, driven by post-pandemic demand, workforce shortages in psychiatry, and growing consumer comfort with remote care. But scale doesn’t equal success. While hundreds of startups promise “AI-powered care” or “therapy on demand,” very few offer proven outcomes, equitable access, or clinical transparency. In 2025, the sector is undergoing a shift: from fragmented offerings to more integrated, evidence-based ecosystems. Below, we examine which models are working, where the cracks are showing, and what innovations might redefine the field, for better or worse. This article builds on our previous piece, Leveraging AI for Mental Health Crisis Intervention, which explored how artificial intelligence is being used to identify and support individuals at risk in moments of acute distress. Here, we take a broader look at the evolving infrastructure of digital mental health—from clinical-grade platforms to consumer-facing tools—and analyze how these technologies are reshaping access, care quality, and accountability at scale. Precision Care: AI-Driven Personalization is Becoming the Norm — But Not Yet the Standard Startups like Spring Health have moved beyond static therapy matching. Their algorithmic triage tools integrate clinical data and user behavior to offer adaptive care plans: self-guided CBT, live coaching, psychiatry, or crisis care. After its Series E in 2024, Spring Health now serves over 10 million employees globally and reports that 70% of users experience improvements in mental health symptoms — such as reduced anxiety or depression — after 6 sessions, though third-party validation remains limited. Other platforms like Ellipsis Health use vocal biomarkers to detect emotional distress in voice recordings, while Kintsugi deploys speech-based machine learning to flag signs of depression or anxiety within 20 seconds. These tools promise earlier detection, but raise privacy concerns, especially in employer-embedded use cases. Insight: AI works best when used to augment—not replace—clinical decisions. But very few tools publish performance benchmarks or account for racial, linguistic, or gender bias in training data. Hybrid Models Are Outperforming "App-Only" Solutions Pure self-help apps are in decline. Instead, platforms are integrating asynchronous tools with access to human clinicians. Hims & Hers, originally a DTC health brand, has now layered in psychiatry, asynchronous screening, and optional live therapy, with pricing transparency ($99 per video session or $49/month for messaging-based care). Notably, they control the full experience: from intake to pharmacy fulfillment. In 2023, the company introduced MedMatch, an AI-powered diagnostic tool that personalizes treatment plans by dynamically pairing individuals with the most appropriate therapeutic or medication-based care, based on clinical guidelines, patient preferences, and outcomes data. Meanwhile, Bend Health focuses on youth mental health through a collaborative care model: combining digital screening with regular feedback loops between parents, teens, and clinicians. It’s one of the few startups that prioritize family engagement — a major gap in most adult-centric platforms. Trend: The platforms seeing the most traction in 2025 are those offering blended care pathways, not single-mode interventions. The most effective combines tech-enabled triage, evidence-based treatment, and sustained follow-up. Equity Gaps Persist — Especially for Non-English, Low-Income, and High-Risk Populations Despite the optimism around “mental health for all,” the reality is that most platforms are built for digitally literate, English-speaking, employer-insured users. In 2023, a significant portion of adults in the U.S. who sought help were unable to access it. Specifically, 45% of those individuals were unable to obtain the necessary support, according to the Federal Reserve Board. Platforms like Wysa attempt to fill this gap through 24/7 multilingual AI chat, used in over 65 countries. It combines anonymous support with optional coaching and integration into primary care systems (notably in the UK and India). However, limited evidence exists on long-term outcomes beyond engagement metrics. Tension: The more scalable a solution is, the more likely it is to sacrifice depth, nuance, or cultural relevance. Access ≠ equity. Regulatory Pressure Is Mounting — and That’s a Good Thing Startups like Cerebral became cautionary tales. Once valued at nearly $5 billion, the company came under investigation by the DOJ and FTC for overprescribing controlled substances and sharing user data with advertisers. In 2023, they were forced to restructure their model and cease prescribing certain medications altogether. While not all companies are as exposed, the landscape is tightening. HIPAA violations, AI transparency rules, and payer scrutiny are forcing startups to act more like healthcare companies — and less like apps. Signal: The winners in 2025 are those willing to build for longevity, not just growth, investing in clinical governance, outcomes measurement, and user protection. Emerging Players to Watch: Platforms Moving Beyond “Therapy as a Service” Some other emerging platforms are pushing the boundaries of what digital mental health can offer beyond the conventional “therapy as a service” model.Uplift is making therapy more social and scalable by offering group-based mental health sessions led by licensed facilitators, creating a peer-supported environment that’s both cost-effective and accessible. Real takes a different approach by providing on-demand psychoeducation and themed therapy pathways — such as those focused on grief, burnout, or relationships — designed for users who seek structure and support without committing to traditional 1:1 sessions. Tava Health is embedding licensed therapists directly into employer health plans, reducing referral friction and making early intervention part of routine workforce wellness. Meanwhile, NOCD is addressing one of the most underserved niches in mental health by delivering clinically validated ERP (exposure and response prevention) therapy for people with OCD, offering measurable outcomes and targeted care through a specialized digital platform.

Conclusion: What the Next Chapter Requires Mental health tech in 2025 is no longer just a space of experimentation — it’s part of the care delivery system. Startups demonstrate how AI and hybrid models can personalize care at scale, while other platforms show the value of niche-specific solutions and constant availability. Meanwhile, companies are rethinking care formats altogether — moving beyond 1:1 therapy into group sessions and thematic journeys. However: Outcome reporting remains opaque: Only a few companies publish validated data on clinical improvement. Most still rely on engagement metrics (e.g., session counts, app usage), which say little about actual patient progress. Access is not yet equity: The vast majority of platforms are built around English-speaking, digitally fluent, and employer-insured populations. There is a clear lack of robust offerings for non-English speakers, older adults, and users without internet or private insurance. Fragmentation is real: While some platforms offer end-to-end care (intake, diagnosis, treatment, follow-up), most still operate in silos. This results in poor handoffs between services and limits integration with primary care or public health systems. To ensure that this growth leads to sustainable, ethical, and equitable care, the next chapter of mental health tech must be defined by: Transparency — Clear, public-facing outcome data, not just product claims. Inclusivity by design — Solutions developed with, not just for, marginalized users. Clinical integrity — Collaboration with licensed professionals, guided by best practices and oversight. System-level integration — Seamless connections with primary care, public payers, and community support. Innovation is no longer enough. It’s time for accountability.

data.title: Bosses’ New Oracle: AI Tools That Spot Employee Distress Before Workers Do
data.ai_summary: Employers are increasingly deploying AI tools that analyze keystrokes, email tone, Slack messages, meeting participation, and biometric signals to detect employee burnout, anxiety, and depression before workers self-report issues. Companies including WTW, Spring Health, AllOne Health, MorphCast, Aware, and HireVue offer platforms that flag risk indicators and deliver automated interventions such as chatbots providing cognitive behavioral exercises, though these tools raise concerns about privacy, bias, and consent. The technology remains largely unregulated in the U.S., while the EU prohibits emotion AI in most workplace contexts, and experts warn that surveillance may undermine the very trust it aims to protect.
